hendrick-theyanoguin.s: Hendrick Theyanoguin was a Mohawk leader and one of the most influential Haudenosaunee spokesmen of his time, a close ally of the British and of William Johnson. He spoke forcefully at the Albany Congress of 1754 about British neglect of the alliance.

hendrik-van-rheede.s: Hendrik van Rheede tot Drakenstein was a Dutch East India Company official and naturalist who served as commander of Malabar from 1670 to 1677. He sponsored and directed the Hortus Malabaricus, a twelve-volume study of the plants of the Malabar coast published in Amsterdam…

henny-eman.s: Henny Eman is an Aruban politician of the Aruban People's Party who became the first Prime Minister of Aruba after it gained separate status within the Kingdom of the Netherlands in 1986. He served from 1986 to 1989 and again from 1994 to 2001.

henriette-of-montbeliard.s: Henriette of Montbéliard was the heiress of the County of Montbéliard, betrothed in 1397 to Eberhard IV of Württemberg, whom she married in 1407. Through her the county passed to the house of Württemberg, which held it until the French Revolution.

henrique-paiva-couceiro.s: Henrique Paiva Couceiro was a Portuguese army officer and colonial administrator, governor-general of Angola from 1907 to 1909, and the leading royalist opponent of the First Portuguese Republic. He led royalist incursions from Spain in 1911 and 1912, and on 19 January 1919…

henry-borwin-iii-lord-of-rostock.n: Henry Borwin III, Lord of Rostock
henry-borwin-iii-lord-of-rostock.s: Henry Borwin III was a member of the Mecklenburg dynasty who received the lands around Rostock when his family's territory was divided in 1229. As the first Lord of Rostock he ruled during the rapid growth of the Hanseatic town, which had received Lübeck law in 1218.

henry-chee-dodge.s: Henry Chee Dodge was a Navajo interpreter, rancher and political leader. He served as head chief of the Navajo from 1884 and became the first chairman of the Navajo Tribal Council when it was created in 1923, chiefly to approve oil leases.

heidelberg-catechism.s: The Heidelberg Catechism is a Reformed Protestant statement of faith in question-and-answer form, published in 1563 at the order of Elector Frederick III of the Palatinate. Written chiefly by Zacharias Ursinus with Caspar Olevian, it made the Palatinate the leading Calvinist…

henry-i-duke-of-brabant.s: Henry I, Duke of Brabant, was the first ruler of the Louvain dynasty to use the title Duke of Brabant, reigning from 1183 to 1235. He founded towns, granted charters and expanded his lands between the Meuse and the Scheldt, though he was defeated by the Prince-Bishop of Liège…

henry-iii-the-white.s: Henry III the White was a Silesian Piast duke, son of Henry II the Pious, who received Wrocław when his father's duchy was divided in 1248. He ruled Wrocław from 1248 to 1266, at first jointly with his brother Władysław, and encouraged German settlement and the town's recovery…

henry-iv-of-plauen.s: Henry IV of Plauen was a member of the Reuss family of Vogtland lords who became Burgrave of Meissen and chancellor of the Kingdom of Bohemia under Ferdinand I. As a reward for his loyalty in the Schmalkaldic War he recovered Plauen and other Vogtland lands in 1547, briefly…

henry-iv-probus.s: Henry IV Probus was Duke of Wrocław from 1270 and High Duke of Poland at Kraków from 1288 to 1290. Raised at the Bohemian court, he was a patron of German poetry and wrote verse in Middle High German himself.

henry-jennings.s: Henry Jennings was an English privateer and pirate based in Jamaica and the Bahamas. In 1716 he raided the Spanish salvage camps of the wrecked 1715 treasure fleet off Florida, and he became one of the leading captains of the pirate community at Nassau.

henry-julius-duke-of-brunswick-luneburg.s: Henry Julius, Duke of Brunswick-Lüneburg, ruled the Principality of Wolfenbüttel from 1589 and was administrator of the Prince-Bishopric of Halberstadt from 1566. A learned prince, he wrote plays, founded a court theatre and served as an adviser to Emperor Rudolf II in Prague.

henry-count-of-portugal.s: Henry, Count of Portugal, was a Burgundian noble who fought for Alfonso VI of León against the Almoravids. Around 1096 he married Alfonso's daughter Teresa and received the County of Portugal, including Coimbra.

henry-parkes.s: Henry Parkes was an English-born journalist and politician who served five times as premier of New South Wales between 1872 and 1891. He promoted free public education and free trade.

henry-raspe.s: Henry Raspe was Landgrave of Thuringia from 1227 to 1247, the last of the Ludowingian dynasty. He first acted as regent for his nephew after the death of his brother Louis IV, husband of Saint Elizabeth of Hungary.

henry-i-duke-of-munsterberg.s: Henry I, Duke of Münsterberg, known as the Elder, was a son of the Bohemian king George of Poděbrady. He held the Silesian Duchy of Münsterberg and the County of Kladsko (Glatz), which he received in 1472, and founded the Poděbrady line of Silesian dukes.

henry-iii-margrave-of-meissen.s: Henry III, Margrave of Meissen, called the Illustrious, was a Wettin prince who ruled Meissen from 1221. Through his mother, a Ludowingian, he claimed Thuringia after the death of Henry Raspe and won it in the War of the Thuringian Succession by 1264.

henry-xiii-duke-of-bavaria.s: Henry XIII, Duke of Bavaria, was a Wittelsbach prince who received Lower Bavaria, with Landshut as his seat, when he and his brother Louis II the Strict divided the duchy in 1255. The partition began the long series of Wittelsbach divisions of Bavaria.

henry-xvi-duke-of-bavaria.s: Henry XVI, Duke of Bavaria, known as the Rich, ruled Bavaria-Landshut from 1393 to 1450. A careful administrator, he built up a great treasure from silver, salt tolls and taxes.

heraclius-the-elder.s: Heraclius the Elder was a Byzantine general of Armenian origin who served against the Persians and became Exarch of Africa at Carthage. In 608 he rebelled against the emperor Phocas, sending his son Heraclius by sea and his nephew Nicetas overland to Egypt.

herbert-ii-count-of-vermandois.s: Herbert II, Count of Vermandois, was a Carolingian descendant and the most powerful magnate of northern France in the 920s. He held King Charles the Simple prisoner at Péronne from 923 until the king's death in 929 and secured the archbishopric of Reims for his young son.

herbert-kitchener.s: Herbert Kitchener was a British army officer who, as Sirdar of the Egyptian army, led the reconquest of Sudan and destroyed the Mahdist army at Omdurman in 1898. He became the first governor-general of Anglo-Egyptian Sudan, later commanded in the Second Boer War and in India,…

herceg-novi.s: Herceg Novi is a fortified port at the entrance to the Bay of Kotor in present-day Montenegro. Founded as Novi in 1382 by Tvrtko I of Bosnia, it was developed by Stjepan Vukčić Kosača, Herceg of Saint Sava, whose title gave the town its name.

herius-asinius.s: Herius Asinius was a commander of the Marrucini, an Italic people of the Adriatic coast, during the Social War against Rome. He led his people's forces on the side of the Italian allies and was killed in battle in 90 BCE.

hermann-balk.s: Hermann Balk was a knight of the Teutonic Order who led its first campaigns in Prussia from 1230, founding Thorn, Kulm and Elbing. After the Livonian Brothers of the Sword were crushed at Saule in 1236, he became the first master of the Order in Livonia in 1237, absorbing the…

hermann-goring.s: Hermann Göring was a leading Nazi, a First World War fighter pilot who became commander of the Luftwaffe and Hitler's designated successor. As minister-president of Prussia from 1933 he founded the Gestapo and used the Prussian police against the regime's opponents.

hermann-of-buxhoeveden.s: Hermann of Buxhoeveden was a German churchman, brother of Bishop Albert of Riga, who was made bishop of the Estonians in 1220. After the capture of Tartu in 1224 he moved his see there, founding the Bishopric of Dorpat, which he ruled until his death.

hermann-von-wissmann.s: Hermann von Wissmann was a German explorer and colonial officer who crossed Central Africa twice in the 1880s. In 1889 he was appointed imperial commissioner to suppress the Abushiri revolt on the East African coast, which he did with a force of African mercenaries.

hermann-wesel.s: Hermann Wesel was the last Bishop of Dorpat, elected in 1554. When the armies of Ivan IV took Dorpat in 1558 at the start of the Livonian War, he surrendered the city and was carried off to Russia, where he died in captivity.

hermanus-steyn.s: Hermanus Steyn was a burgher of the Swellendam district of the Dutch Cape Colony. In June 1795, after the settlers expelled the Dutch East India Company's landdrost, he was chosen president of their assembly of national representatives in the short-lived Swellendam Republic.

hermenegildo-gutierrez.s: Hermenegildo Gutiérrez was a Galician noble in the service of Alfonso III of Asturias. In 878 he captured Coimbra on the Mondego from the Emirate of Córdoba and became the first count of the frontier County of Coimbra.

hernandarias.s: Hernandarias, Hernando Arias de Saavedra, was born in Asunción and was the first American-born governor of the Río de la Plata, holding office several times between 1592 and 1618. He explored the interior, promoted cattle ranching and invited the Jesuits to found missions…

herod-agrippa-i.s: Herod Agrippa I was a grandson of Herod the Great, raised in Rome and a friend of the emperors Caligula and Claudius. Caligula gave him the former Tetrarchy of Philip with the title of king in 37, and by 41 Claudius had added Judaea and Samaria, reuniting his grandfather's realm.

hibatullah-akhundzada.s: Hibatullah Akhundzada is an Afghan cleric and Islamic jurist who became leader of the Taliban in 2016. After the Taliban took Kabul in August 2021 and restored the Islamic Emirate of Afghanistan, he became its supreme leader.

hiero-ii-of-syracuse.s: Hiero II of Syracuse was a general who seized power in Syracuse and took the title of king after defeating the Mamertines at the Longanus river around 265 BCE. Early in the First Punic War he allied with Rome in 263 BCE and remained a loyal ally until his death.

high-king-of-ireland.s: The High King of Ireland, Ard Rí in Irish, was the title claimed by kings who asserted supremacy over the island's many kingdoms. Long associated with Tara and the Uí Néill, it became a real prize from the late 10th century, when Brian Bóruma of Munster took it in 1002.

hikayat-merong-mahawangsa.s: The Hikayat Merong Mahawangsa, also called the Kedah Annals, is a Malay chronicle of the kingdom of Kedah. It traces the royal line to Merong Mahawangsa, a legendary founder, and describes the ruler's conversion to Islam.

hikayat-tanah-hitu.s: The Hikayat Tanah Hitu is a Malay chronicle of Hitu on Ambon Island, written in the mid-17th century by Imam Rijali, a Hitu leader who fled the Dutch. It recounts the origins of Hitu's rulers, the coming of Islam and the wars against the Portuguese and the Dutch East India…

hill-complex-great-zimbabwe.s: The Hill Complex is the oldest part of Great Zimbabwe, a group of stone enclosures built among the granite boulders of a steep hill overlooking the valley. Construction began in the 11th or 12th century, and the complex is thought to have been the residence of the kings and a…

himmat-singh-of-idar.s: Himmat Singh was the last Maharaja of Idar, a Rajput princely state in northern Gujarat, ruling from 1931 to 1949. The capital Ahmednagar was renamed Himmatnagar after him.

hinrich-lohse.s: Hinrich Lohse was a Nazi politician, Gauleiter of Schleswig-Holstein from 1925. From 1941 to 1944 he was Reich Commissioner of Reichskommissariat Ostland, governing the occupied Baltic states and western Belarus from Riga, where his administration took part in the persecution…

hiralal-shastri.s: Hiralal Shastri was an Indian independence activist and social reformer from Jaipur, founder of the Vanasthali Vidyapith women's college. In 1949 he became the first chief minister of the United State of Rajasthan, leading the elected ministry that governed the union of former…

hisham-ii.s: Hisham II was the third Umayyad Caliph of Córdoba, succeeding as a child in 976. Real power lay with the hajib Almanzor and his sons, while Hisham was kept secluded.

hasankeyf.s: Hasankeyf, medieval Hisn Kayfa, is an ancient town on the Tigris in south-eastern Turkey. It was the seat of the Artuqids from 1102 and of a branch of the Ayyubids from 1232 into the 15th century, who built its great bridge, mosques and palaces.

hjalmar-mae.s: Hjalmar Mäe was an Estonian politician of the far-right Vaps movement who headed the Estonian Self-Administration set up by the German occupiers from 1941 to 1944. His administration operated under the Generalkommissariat Estland within Reichskommissariat Ostland.

ho-chi-minh-trail.s: The Ho Chi Minh Trail was a network of roads, tracks and river routes running from North Vietnam through Laos and Cambodia to South Vietnam. North Vietnam used it from 1959 to send troops and supplies to the southern insurgency.

ho-han-thuong.s: Hồ Hán Thương was the second and last emperor of the Hồ dynasty of Vietnam, reigning from 1401 to 1407, while his father Hồ Quý Ly kept real power. Their state of Đại Ngu fell to the invading Ming army in 1407, and father and son were captured and taken to China, beginning two…

hoa-hao.s: Hòa Hảo is a Vietnamese Buddhist reform movement founded in 1939 by Huỳnh Phú Sổ in the Mekong Delta village of Hòa Hảo. It stresses simple lay devotion over temples and clergy and quickly won a mass peasant following.

hojo-ujimasa.s: Hōjō Ujimasa was the fourth head of the Later Hōjō clan, ruling much of the Kantō from Odawara. He continued his father Ujiyasu's wars against the Takeda and Uesugi.

hojo-ujiyasu.s: Hōjō Ujiyasu was the third head of the Later Hōjō clan and one of the leading Sengoku warlords. His night attack at Kawagoe in 1546 broke a coalition of the Uesugi and made the Hōjō masters of the Kantō.

holy-cross-minster.s: The Holy Cross Minster is the main church of Schwäbisch Gmünd in southern Germany. Its choir, begun in 1351 by Heinrich Parler, is an early and influential example of the late Gothic hall church in Germany.

holy-land.s: The Holy Land is the region between the Jordan River and the Mediterranean, roughly ancient Israel and Palestine, held sacred by Jews, Christians and Muslims. Medieval Europeans used the term for the places of Christ's life, the goal of pilgrimage and of the Crusades.

honda-tadakatsu.s: Honda Tadakatsu was one of the four great generals of Tokugawa Ieyasu, famed for fighting in dozens of battles without being seriously wounded. After the Battle of Sekigahara in 1600 he received the Kuwana domain with 100,000 koku, where he rebuilt the castle and laid out the…

honda-tadamasa.s: Honda Tadamasa was a daimyo, eldest son of Honda Tadakatsu, who succeeded to Kuwana and in 1617 was moved to the Himeji domain. His son married Senhime, granddaughter of Tokugawa Ieyasu, tying the family closely to the shogunate.

hong-rengan.s: Hong Rengan was a cousin of Hong Xiuquan who learned of Western ways from missionaries in Hong Kong. Arriving at Nanjing in 1859, he became prime minister of the Taiping Heavenly Kingdom with the title Shield King and proposed railways, banks, a postal service and newspapers…

horio-yoshiharu.s: Horio Yoshiharu was a daimyo who served Toyotomi Hideyoshi and then sided with Tokugawa Ieyasu. After Sekigahara his family received Izumo and Oki, and he directed the building of Matsue castle on Lake Shinji, completed in 1611, the year he died.

hosein-qoli-khan-qajar.s: Hosein Qoli Khan Qajar was the last governor, or sardar, of the Erivan Khanate for Qajar Iran, appointed in 1807. He defended Erivan against Russian attacks and built the Sardar's Palace in its fortress.

hosseinqoli-khan-bakhtiari.s: Hosseinqoli Khan Bakhtiari was a chief of the Haft Lang Bakhtiari who united the confederation of the Zagros under his leadership. In 1867 the Qajar government recognised him as ilkhan, paramount chief, of all the Bakhtiari.

hoshang-shah.s: Hoshang Shah was the second Sultan of Malwa, reigning from 1406 to 1435, son of the dynasty's founder Dilawar Khan Ghuri. He moved the capital from Dhar to the hill fortress of Mandu, which he fortified, and fought Gujarat and neighbouring Rajput states.

hoshina-masayuki.s: Hoshina Masayuki was a son of the shogun Tokugawa Hidetada and half-brother of Iemitsu, raised in the Hoshina family. Given Aizu in 1643, he founded the line that held it until 1868, and he served as guardian of the young shogun Ietsuna.

hosni-mubarak.s: Hosni Mubarak was an Egyptian air force commander who became vice-president and, after Anwar Sadat's assassination in 1981, president of Egypt. He kept the peace with Israel, relied on emergency laws and close ties with the United States, and ruled for almost thirty years.

hosokawa-shigekata.s: Hosokawa Shigekata was daimyo of Kumamoto from 1747 and one of the noted domain reformers of the Edo period. He restored the domain's finances, reorganised its administration and criminal law, and promoted local products.

hosokawa-tadaoki.s: Hosokawa Tadaoki was a samurai and tea master who fought for Tokugawa Ieyasu at Sekigahara in 1600. His wife, the Christian Hosokawa Gracia, died rather than be taken hostage by Ieyasu's enemies.

hosokawa-tadatoshi.s: Hosokawa Tadatoshi was the son of Hosokawa Tadaoki and daimyo of Kokura, transferred in 1632 to Kumamoto in Higo with 540,000 koku after the shogunate removed the Katō family. His family held Kumamoto until 1871.

hotu-matua.s: Hotu Matuʻa is the legendary founding chief of Rapa Nui (Easter Island). Island tradition says he sailed from a homeland called Hiva, landed at Anakena Bay and divided the island among his sons, ancestors of its clans.

hotula-khan.s: Hotula Khan was a khan of the Khamag Mongol confederation in the mid-12th century, son of Khabul Khan and uncle of Yesügei. Elected after the Tatars handed Ambaghai Khan to the Jin, he waged wars of revenge against the Tatars.

hovhannes-kajaznuni.s: Hovhannes Kajaznuni was an Armenian architect and leader of the Armenian Revolutionary Federation who served as the first prime minister of the First Republic of Armenia from 1918 to 1919. In 1923 he published a critical report on his party's record.

hubert-lyautey.s: Hubert Lyautey was a French general and the first resident-general of the French protectorate in Morocco, from 1912 to 1925. He ruled through the sultan and the makhzen, made Rabat the capital, built new European towns beside the old medinas and conducted long campaigns in the…

hubert-maga.s: Hubert Maga was a schoolteacher from northern Dahomey who became one of the colony's three leading politicians. He was the first president of independent Dahomey from 1960 until a coup in 1963, and returned as head of a rotating presidential council in 1970, before Mathieu…

hubert-murray.s: Hubert Murray was an Australian lawyer who governed Papua as lieutenant-governor from 1908 until his death in 1940. His long administration was paternalistic, restricting land alienation and forced labour while limiting economic development.

hudhayl-ibn-khalaf-ibn-razin.s: Hudhayl ibn Khalaf ibn Razin was a Berber chief of the Banu Razin who made Albarracín independent around 1012, as the Caliphate of Córdoba broke apart. He ruled the mountainous Taifa of Albarracín until 1045, keeping it independent between the larger taifas of Toledo, Zaragoza…

hudson-valley.s: The Hudson Valley is the valley of the Hudson River in New York, running north from New York City towards Albany. The Dutch settled it as the core of New Netherland, granting large patroonships such as Rensselaerswyck.

hugh-low.s: Hugh Low was a British colonial administrator and naturalist. He served in Labuan from 1848, first as colonial secretary, and in 1851 made the first recorded ascent of Mount Kinabalu's summit plateau.

hugh-maguire-lord-of-fermanagh.s: Hugh Maguire was Lord of Fermanagh from 1589 and one of the Irish leaders of the Nine Years' War against English rule. His resistance to an English sheriff began the conflict in 1593, and he won a victory at the Ford of the Biscuits in 1594.

hugh-of-bruyeres.s: Hugh of Bruyeres was a crusader knight from Champagne who received the Barony of Karytaina, one of the largest fiefs of the Principality of Achaea, around 1209. He held the Skorta highlands of the upper Alpheios valley.

hugh-of-ibelin.s: Hugh of Ibelin was the eldest son of Barisan of Ibelin and lord of Ibelin and Ramla in the Kingdom of Jerusalem. He was captured by Nur ad-Din's forces in 1157 and ransomed, and he married Agnes of Courtenay, former wife of King Amalric.

hugh-of-vermandois.s: Hugh of Vermandois was a younger son of King Henry I of France who became Count of Vermandois by marriage to its heiress Adelaide. He was among the leaders of the First Crusade, but returned to France after the capture of Antioch in 1098.

hugh-roe-macmahon.s: Hugh Roe MacMahon was lord of Monaghan, the MacMahon lordship of Oriel in Ulster. After he was recognised by the English administration, the Lord Deputy William Fitzwilliam had him arrested, tried and hanged in 1590.

hugo-chavez.s: Hugo Chávez was a Venezuelan army officer who led a failed coup in 1992 and was elected president in 1998. A new constitution in 1999 renamed the country the Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela.

hugo-von-montfort.s: Hugo von Montfort was a count of the Bregenz line of the Montfort family and a Habsburg official who served as governor of Styria. He is best known as a poet: his German songs, letters and speeches, many with melodies, survive in a manuscript at Heidelberg and make him one of…

hujr-akil-al-murar.s: Hujr Akil al-Murar was a chief of the Kinda tribe and the founder of the Kingdom of Kinda in central Arabia. In the 5th century the Himyarite kings installed him as king over the Ma'add tribes of Najd.

huldrych-zwingli.s: Huldrych Zwingli was a Swiss priest and leader of the Reformation in Zürich. After serving as parish priest at Glarus, he moved to Zürich in 1519, where his preaching led the city to abolish the Mass in 1525.

humbert-ii-of-viennois.s: Humbert II of Viennois was the last independent Dauphin of the Viennois, ruling from 1333. He founded a university at Grenoble in 1339 and led a papal crusade to Smyrna in 1345 to 1347.

humbert-i-count-of-savoy.s: Humbert I, known as White-Hands, was a noble of the Kingdom of Arles who held lands around Maurienne and Savoy from about 1003. He gained control of Alpine passes and was rewarded by Emperor Conrad II for his support.

humphrey-ii-of-toron.s: Humphrey II of Toron was lord of Toron and constable of the Kingdom of Jerusalem from 1152. He was trusted as a negotiator by Muslim rulers, including Saladin, and fought in many campaigns.

hundred-years-war.s: The Hundred Years' War was a series of conflicts between the kings of England and France from 1337 to 1453, caused by disputes over Gascony and English claims to the French crown. English victories at Crécy, Poitiers and Agincourt were reversed after Joan of Arc's intervention…

hurricane-irma.s: Hurricane Irma was a Category 5 Atlantic hurricane that struck the northern Caribbean in September 2017, one of the strongest recorded in the open Atlantic. It destroyed most buildings on Barbuda, forcing the evacuation of the whole island, and devastated Sint Maarten and…

hurricane-maria.s: Hurricane Maria was a Category 5 hurricane that struck the eastern Caribbean in September 2017, two weeks after Hurricane Irma. It caused catastrophic damage on Dominica and then crossed Puerto Rico, destroying its power grid; studies estimated around 3,000 deaths there in the…

husain-shah-langah.s: Husain Shah Langah was the most important ruler of the Langah Sultanate of Multan in the second half of the 15th century. During a reign of about three decades he repelled attacks by Bahlul Lodi of Delhi and extended his rule along the Indus towards Sindh, while Multan…

husam-al-din-choban.s: Husam al-Din Choban was a commander of the Seljuk Sultanate of Rum who received the frontier district of Kastamonu in the early 13th century. Around 1220 he led the Seljuk naval expedition across the Black Sea against Sudak in the Crimea.

husayn-ali-khan-of-quba.s: Husayn Ali Khan was khan of Quba in the north-eastern Caucasus. After the death of Nader Shah in 1747 he ruled as an effectively independent khan and moved his seat to the new town of Quba.

husayn-ibn-ahmad-al-habili.s: Husayn ibn Ahmad al-Habili was the sharif of Beihan, a small emirate on the frontier between the Aden Protectorate and Yemen. One of Britain's firmest allies in southern Arabia, he resisted Yemeni claims to the border in the 1950s and was a founding figure of the Federation of…

husayn-ibn-salamah.s: Husayn ibn Salamah was a Nubian freedman who served as regent and chief minister of the Ziyadid dynasty of Zabid in Yemen in the late 10th century. He held the real power in the state, built mosques and fortified towns, and constructed roads and wells linking Zabid with Mecca…

husayn-sufi.s: Husayn Sufi was a leader of the Qungrat tribe who made himself independent ruler of Khwarazm around 1361, as the Golden Horde fell into civil war. Ruling from Urgench, he founded the Sufi dynasty and seized southern Khwarazm, including Khiva and Kath.

huseyngulu-khan.s: Huseyngulu Khan was the last khan of Baku, ruling from 1792. In 1806 the Russian commander Pavel Tsitsianov came to accept the city's surrender and was killed at its gates by the khan's men.

huynh-tan-phat.s: Huỳnh Tấn Phát was a Vietnamese architect and communist politician who helped found the National Liberation Front. From 1969 he was chairman of the Provisional Revolutionary Government of the Republic of South Vietnam, the southern insurgency's government during the Paris…

house-of-la-marck.s: The House of La Marck was a noble family from the County of Mark in Westphalia, one of whose branches rose to power in the Ardennes from the 15th century. Its members gained control of the Duchy of Bouillon and the principality of Sedan, which they ruled as near-independent…

henri-de-la-tour-d-auvergne-viscount-of-.n: Henri de La Tour d'Auvergne, Viscount of Turenne
henri-de-la-tour-d-auvergne-viscount-of-.s: Henri de La Tour d'Auvergne, Viscount of Turenne, was one of the greatest French generals, born at Sedan, the son of its sovereign prince. He commanded in the Thirty Years' War, the Fronde and the Franco-Dutch War, becoming Marshal General of France.

hendrik-verwoerd.s: Hendrik Verwoerd was a South African National Party politician, minister of native affairs from 1950 and prime minister from 1958 to 1966. He was the principal architect of grand apartheid, including the Bantustan system.

hans-adam-i-prince-of-liechtenstein.s: Hans-Adam I, born Johann Adam Andreas, was prince of Liechtenstein from 1684 to 1712 and a wealthy Austrian magnate. To win his family a seat in the Imperial Diet he bought the Lordship of Schellenberg in 1699 and the County of Vaduz in 1712, which were united in 1719 as the…

hedwig-of-silesia.s: Hedwig of Silesia was a daughter of the counts of Andechs, dukes of Merania, and wife of Duke Henry I the Bearded of Silesia. With her husband she founded the Cistercian convent at Trzebnica and supported German settlement and new towns.

heidelberg-university.s: Heidelberg University was founded in 1386 by Rupert I, Elector Palatine, and is the oldest university in present-day Germany. It was a centre of humanism and, after the Electoral Palatinate became Calvinist, of Reformed theology, associated with the Heidelberg Catechism of 1563.

hero-and-leander.s: Hero and Leander is a Greek myth about two lovers on either side of the Hellespont. Leander, a youth of Abydos, swam across the strait each night to Hero, a priestess of Aphrodite at Sestos, guided by a lamp in her tower, until a storm put out the light and he drowned, and…

hamzah-fansuri.s: Hamzah Fansuri was a Sufi poet and scholar from Sumatra, active in Aceh in the late 16th century. His mystical poems, written in the syair form, are among the earliest known works of Malay literature and made Malay a language of Sufi thought.

hermes.s: Hermes was a Greek god, son of Zeus and Maia, the messenger of the gods and the guide of souls to the underworld. He protected travellers, herdsmen, merchants and thieves, and was shown with a winged hat or sandals and a herald's staff.

heracles.s: Heracles, called Hercules by the Romans, was the greatest hero of Greek myth, a son of Zeus and the mortal Alcmene. He was famed for his strength and for the Twelve Labours imposed on him by Eurystheus, and after his death he was received among the gods.

hokkaido.s: Hokkaido is the second-largest and northernmost of Japan's main islands. Long known to the Japanese as Ezo, it was the homeland of the Ainu, while the Matsumae clan controlled trade from a foothold in the south.

honshu.s: Honshu is the largest of the islands of Japan and the seventh-largest island in the world. It holds most of the country's population and its historic centres, including Kyoto, Nara, Osaka and Tokyo.

horatii-and-curiatii.s: The Horatii and Curiatii were two sets of triplet brothers who, according to Livy, fought a duel to decide the war between Rome and Alba Longa under King Tullus Hostilius in the mid-7th century BCE. Two Roman Horatii fell, but the survivor killed all three Albans, and Alba…

hindko.s: Hindko is a group of Indo-Aryan dialects spoken in north-western Pakistan, especially in the Hazara region and the city of Peshawar in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, and in parts of northern Punjab. Closely related to Punjabi and Saraiki, it is spoken by several million people, many of…

hagnon.s: Hagnon was an Athenian general and politician who founded the colony of Amphipolis on the Strymon river in 437 BCE. He later served as a general in the Peloponnesian War, and in 413 BCE he was one of the probouloi, the board of commissioners appointed after the Sicilian disaster.

house-of-este.s: The House of Este was an Italian princely family, named after the town of Este near Padua, which ruled Ferrara from the 13th century and Modena and Reggio from 1288. Its rulers, raised to dukes in the 15th century, made Ferrara a leading Renaissance court, patronising Ariosto…

hermes-of-andros.s: The Hermes of Andros is a marble statue of the god Hermes as guide of souls, found in 1832 at Palaiopolis, the ancient city of Andros, in the Cyclades. A Roman-period copy of a 4th-century BCE original related to the style of Praxiteles, it probably stood on a tomb.

hulwan.s: Hulwan was an ancient and medieval town at the foot of the Zagros mountains, near modern Sarpol-e Zahab in western Iran, where the main road from Mesopotamia climbed onto the Iranian plateau. An important Sasanian centre, it was taken by the Arabs around 640 and became a…

history-of-the-great-island-of-madagasca.n: History of the Great Island of Madagascar
history-of-the-great-island-of-madagasca.s: The History of the Great Island of Madagascar (Histoire de la grande isle Madagascar) is a book by Étienne de Flacourt, French governor of Fort-Dauphin, published in 1658. Drawing on his years in the colony from 1648, it describes the geography, plants, animals, peoples and…

herisau.s: Herisau is a town in north-eastern Switzerland and the capital of the half-canton of Appenzell Ausserrhoden. A market centre of the linen and later cotton trade, it grew into the canton's largest town.

hundwil.s: Hundwil is a village in the Swiss half-canton of Appenzell Ausserrhoden. After the division of Appenzell in 1597 it alternated with Trogen as the meeting place of Ausserrhoden's Landsgemeinde, the open-air assembly of citizens, until voters abolished the assembly in 1997.

hauran.s: The Hauran is a volcanic plateau and fertile plain in south-western Syria, extending into northern Jordan, between the Golan Heights and the Jabal al-Druze. Long a granary for Damascus, it was ruled in turn by Aramaeans, Nabataeans, Romans and Ghassanids, and its black basalt…

humayun.s: Humayun was the second Mughal emperor, son and successor of Babur, who ruled from 1530 to 1540 and again in 1555–1556. Defeated by Sher Shah Suri at Chausa in 1539 and Kannauj in 1540, he lost his kingdom and spent years as a fugitive in Sindh, where his son Akbar was born in…

hethum-i.s: Hethum I was king of the Armenian Kingdom of Cilicia from 1226 to 1270, founder of the Hethumid line of kings. He submitted to the Mongols and travelled to their capital Karakorum in 1254 to secure an alliance against the Mamluks.

hromkla.s: Hromkla, Turkish Rumkale, is a fortress on a crag above the Euphrates in south-eastern Turkey. From 1149 it was the seat of the Catholicos of the Armenian Church and a centre of manuscript illumination, where Toros Roslin worked.

house-of-lusignan.s: The House of Lusignan was a French noble family from Poitou, lords of Lusignan and counts of La Marche and Angoulême. Through Guy of Lusignan it gained the crowns of Jerusalem and Cyprus at the end of the 12th century, and it ruled Cyprus until the late 15th century.

harput.s: Harput is a historic hill town in eastern Turkey, just north of the city of Elazığ. Its castle commanded the plain of the upper Euphrates and was held from the early 12th century by an Artuqid branch, whose ruler Belek imprisoned King Baldwin II of Jerusalem there in 1123.

harput-ulu-mosque.s: The Harput Ulu Mosque is a mosque in the old town of Harput in eastern Turkey, built in 1156–1157 under the Artuqid ruler Fakhr al-Din Qara Arslan. One of the oldest mosques in Anatolia, it is built of brick and stone, and its minaret leans noticeably.

husam-al-din-timurtash.s: Husam al-Din Timurtash was the Artuqid ruler of Mardin from 1122 to 1154, a son of Ilghazi. He briefly held Aleppo after his father's death, released the captive King Baldwin II of Jerusalem for a ransom in 1124, and kept Mardin and Mayyafariqin by balancing between the…

humban.s: Humban was one of the chief gods of ancient Elam, in south-western Iran, worshipped from the 3rd millennium BCE. He was regarded as a lord of the sky and closely linked with kingship, and his name formed part of many royal names, such as Humban-nikash and Humban-haltash.

hodh.s: The Hodh is a large semi-arid basin in south-eastern Mauritania, bordering Mali, now divided into the regions of Hodh Ech Chargui and Hodh El Gharbi. A land of pastoral nomads and oases, it was dominated by Hassani Arab emirates such as the Awlad Mbarak and includes the old…

hovhannes-smbat-iii.s: Hovhannes-Smbat III was the Bagratid king of Armenia who ruled from Ani from about 1020 to 1041, after the death of his father Gagik I. He shared the kingdom with his brother Ashot IV, who held the eastern lands.

hubert-ingraham.s: Hubert Ingraham is a Bahamian politician who served as prime minister of the Bahamas from 1992 to 2002 and again from 2007 to 2012. A former minister in Lynden Pindling's Progressive Liberal Party government, he was dismissed from the cabinet in 1984, later joined the…

hurricane-dorian.s: Hurricane Dorian was an Atlantic hurricane that struck the northern Bahamas as a Category 5 storm in September 2019. It stalled over the Abaco Islands and Grand Bahama for more than a day, with sustained winds near 185 miles per hour, causing catastrophic storm surges and…

haft-lang.s: The Haft Lang is one of the two main divisions of the Bakhtiari tribal confederation of south-western Iran, the other being the Chahar Lang. From the 19th century its leading families, descended from Hossein Qoli Khan, supplied the ilkhans, or paramount chiefs, of the whole…

hannibal-mago.s: Hannibal Mago was a Carthaginian general of the Magonid family, grandson of the Hamilcar who had died at the Battle of Himera in 480 BCE. In 409 BCE he led a large army to Sicily, where he stormed Selinous and then destroyed Himera, reportedly executing 3,000 prisoners to…

hussain-muhammad-ershad.s: Hussain Muhammad Ershad was a Bangladeshi army chief who seized power in a bloodless coup in March 1982 and ruled as chief martial law administrator and then president until 1990. He founded the Jatiya Party, made Islam the state religion in 1988 and decentralised…

hafizullah-amin.s: Hafizullah Amin was an Afghan communist leader of the Khalq faction of the People's Democratic Party of Afghanistan, which seized power in the Saur Revolution of April 1978. In September 1979 he ousted his rival Nur Muhammad Taraki, who was then killed, and became president.

huesca.s: Huesca is a city in Aragon in north-eastern Spain, at the foot of the Pyrenees. The Roman Osca was the base of the rebel general Sertorius, and in the Middle Ages it was a Muslim stronghold of the Upper March, held at times by the Banu Qasi and later part of the taifa of…

himilce.s: Himilce, also called Imilce, was an Iberian woman from Castulo, in the upper Guadalquivir valley, who married the Carthaginian general Hannibal. Livy records that Hannibal's wife came from Castulo, and the poet Silius Italicus gives her name.

hispania-ulterior.s: Hispania Ulterior ('Further Spain') was a Roman province created in 197 BCE in the south and west of the Iberian Peninsula, centred on the Baetis (Guadalquivir) valley, with Corduba as its main city. Under Augustus it was divided into the provinces of Baetica and Lusitania.

halba.s: The Halba are an Adivasi community of central India, living mainly in Chhattisgarh, especially the Bastar region, and in neighbouring Odisha and Maharashtra. Traditionally farmers, some of them served the Rajas of Bastar.

high-commission-territories.s: The High Commission Territories were the three British dependencies of Basutoland, the Bechuanaland Protectorate and Swaziland, governed through the British High Commissioner for southern Africa rather than the Colonial Office. South Africa long hoped to absorb them, but…

hambukushu.s: The Hambukushu are a Bantu-speaking people living along the Okavango River in north-western Botswana, north-eastern Namibia and south-eastern Angola. Many moved into the Okavango panhandle in the 18th and 19th centuries, and they came under the authority of the Batawana.

huerva.s: The Huerva is a river of Aragon in north-eastern Spain, a right-bank tributary of the Ebro about 130 km long. It rises in the Iberian System and flows north-east to join the Ebro at Zaragoza.

husain-shahi-dynasty.s: The Husain Shahi dynasty ruled the Bengal Sultanate from 1494 to 1538. Its founder, Alauddin Husain Shah, restored order after a period of palace coups and extended Bengal's power into Assam, Odisha and Bihar.

hammuda-ibn-ali.s: Hammuda ibn Ali, also called Hammuda Pasha, was the Husainid bey of Tunis from 1782 to 1814. His reign is regarded as the high point of the dynasty: Tunis grew prosperous from trade and corsair activity, he repelled a Venetian naval campaign, and in 1807 he defeated the…

husainid-dynasty.s: The Husainid dynasty ruled Tunisia as beys from 1705, when the cavalry officer Husayn ibn Ali seized power during an invasion from Algiers, until 1957. Nominally under Ottoman sovereignty, the beys governed largely independently and in the 19th century attempted modernising…

hamidullah-khan.s: Hamidullah Khan was the last ruling Nawab of Bhopal, from 1926 to 1949, succeeding his mother Sultan Jahan Begum. He was twice chancellor of the Chamber of Princes and opposed the merger of the princely states into India, holding out until 1949, when Bhopal became a centrally…

hautes-pyrenees.s: Hautes-Pyrénées is a department in south-western France on the Spanish border, in the Occitanie region, with Tarbes as its prefecture. It covers the central Pyrenees and the upper Adour valley, and roughly corresponds to the old County of Bigorre.

house-of-billung.s: The House of Billung was a Saxon noble family whose members were dukes of Saxony from the 10th century until 1106. Its founder, Hermann Billung, was given command of the frontier against the Slavs along the lower Elbe by Otto I around 936, the region later called the Billung…

hadad-yithi.s: Hadad-yith'i was a ruler of Guzana, the Aramaean kingdom of Bit-Bahiani in north-eastern Syria, in the 9th century BCE. He is known from a life-size basalt statue found at Tell Fekheriye in 1979, which carries a dedication in both Assyrian Akkadian, calling him governor, and…

hercynian-forest.s: The Hercynian Forest was the name given by Greek and Roman writers to the great forest of central Europe, stretching east from the Rhine across southern Germany to the Carpathians. Julius Caesar wrote that it took nine days to cross.

host-of-loyal-zaporozhians.s: The Host of Loyal Zaporozhians was a Cossack army formed in 1787 by Grigory Potemkin from former Zaporozhian Cossacks, whose Sich had been destroyed by Russia in 1775. It fought for Russia in the Russo-Turkish War of 1787–1792, including the sieges of Ochakiv and Izmail.

hellenica-oxyrhynchia.s: The Hellenica Oxyrhynchia is a Greek historical work known from papyrus fragments found at Oxyrhynchus in Egypt and first published in 1908. Its unknown author continued Thucydides, and the surviving parts cover events of 409 and 396–395 BCE in detail.

hailongtun.s: Hailongtun is a mountain fortress near Zunyi in Guizhou, China, built in 1257 by the Southern Song against the Mongols and later the seat of the Yang chieftains of Bozhou. It was stormed by a Ming army under Li Hualong in 1600, ending the rebellion of Yang Yinglong.

humberto-castelo-branco.s: Humberto Castelo Branco was a Brazilian marshal who led the military coup of 1964 against President João Goulart and became the first president of the military regime, serving until 1967. He used Institutional Acts to purge opponents, abolished the old parties and created a…

humber.s: The Humber is a large tidal estuary on the east coast of northern England, formed by the meeting of the rivers Ouse and Trent and flowing into the North Sea. Since early times it has been a major boundary and routeway: the Anglo-Saxon kingdom of Northumbria took its name from…

hurricane-hattie.s: Hurricane Hattie was a powerful hurricane that struck British Honduras on 31 October 1961. Its winds and storm surge devastated Belize City and other coastal towns and killed hundreds of people.

honiara.s: Honiara is the capital of the Solomon Islands, on the north coast of Guadalcanal. It grew from the base built by American forces during the Guadalcanal campaign of 1942–1943 and replaced Tulagi as the capital of the British Solomon Islands Protectorate after the Second World…

hassanal-bolkiah.s: Hassanal Bolkiah is the sultan of Brunei, who succeeded his father Omar Ali Saifuddien III in 1967. He led the country to full independence from Britain in 1984 and has since also served as prime minister and held other key ministries.

hada-chauhans.s: The Hadas are a branch of the Chauhan clan of Rajputs, who ruled the region of south-eastern Rajasthan named Hadoti after them. Rao Deva took Bundi in 1342, and a junior line founded the separate state of Kota in the 17th century.

hadoti.s: Hadoti is a region of south-eastern Rajasthan, India, around the cities of Kota, Bundi, Baran and Jhalawar. It takes its name from the Hada Chauhan Rajputs, who ruled the states of Bundi and Kota there from the 14th century.

house-of-hohenzollern.s: The House of Hohenzollern is a German dynasty named after its castle near Hechingen in Swabia. Its Franconian line, descended from Frederick of Zollern, burgrave of Nuremberg from 1192, gained Brandenburg in 1415 and later ruled Prussia and, from 1871 to 1918, the German Empire.

house-of-raabs.s: The Raabs were an Austrian noble family, named after Raabs an der Thaya in Lower Austria, who held the burgraviate of Nuremberg from about 1105. When their male line died out around 1190, the office passed through the heiress Sophia of Raabs to her husband Frederick of…

hispaniola.s: Hispaniola is the second-largest island of the Caribbean, in the Greater Antilles, shared today by Haiti in the west and the Dominican Republic in the east. Called Ayiti by the Taíno, it was reached by Columbus in 1492 and became the first base of Spanish colonisation in the…

huascar.s: Huáscar was Sapa Inca of the Inca Empire from about 1527 to 1532, ruling from Cuzco after the death of his father Huayna Capac. His half-brother Atahualpa, based in Quito, rose against him, and in the civil war that followed Atahualpa's generals defeated and captured Huáscar…

house-of-zahringen.s: The House of Zähringen was a noble dynasty of south-western Germany, named after Zähringen Castle near Freiburg im Breisgau. Its dukes founded towns including Freiburg im Breisgau, Fribourg and Bern, and governed much of western Switzerland as rectors of Burgundy.

hofe-district.s: Höfe is a district of the Swiss canton of Schwyz on the southern shore of Lake Zurich, made up of the municipalities of Wollerau, Freienbach and Feusisberg. It belonged to the abbey of Einsiedeln and to Zürich, which ceded it to Schwyz in 1440 after the Old Zürich War.

henry-vii-of-germany.s: Henry (VII) was the eldest son of Emperor Frederick II and ruled Germany as king from 1220 while his father lived in Italy. In 1231 he bought the valley of Uri back from the Habsburgs and granted it imperial immediacy, a key step towards Swiss independence.

himiko.s: Himiko was a queen of Yamatai, the leading polity of the Wa people of Japan, known from the Chinese Records of the Three Kingdoms. She ruled as a shaman queen and sent envoys to the Cao Wei court in 239, receiving the title 'Queen of Wa Friendly to Wei' and a gold seal.

hatuey.s: Hatuey was a Taíno chief from Hispaniola who fled to eastern Cuba and led resistance against the Spanish conquest under Diego Velázquez de Cuéllar. Captured, he was burned alive in 1512.

havana.s: Havana is the capital and largest city of Cuba, founded by the Spanish in 1515 and moved to its present site on a sheltered bay around 1519. It became the gathering port of the treasure fleets and was heavily fortified; it was the capital from 1607.

hotimir.s: Hotimir was a prince of Carantania from about 752 to 769, raised as a Christian hostage in Bavaria. He supported the mission sent by Bishop Virgil of Salzburg under Modestus, which built the first churches in the country, including at Maria Saal.

hertfordshire.s: Hertfordshire is a county of south-east England, immediately north of London, with Hertford as its county town. In the late Iron Age it was the heartland of the Catuvellauni, and the Roman town of Verulamium stood there beside modern St Albans.

huallaga-river.s: The Huallaga is a river of central and northern Peru, about 1,140 km long, rising in the Andes near Cerro de Pasco and flowing north past Huánuco and through the San Martín region to join the Marañón. Its forests bordered the lands of the Chachapoya culture to the west.

hammira-deva.s: Hammira Deva was the Chauhan king of Ranthambore in eastern Rajasthan from about 1283 to 1301, the last ruler of the Chahamanas of Ranastambhapura. He raided Malwa and Mewar, and sheltered Mongol rebels who had fled Alauddin Khalji's army; Alauddin besieged Ranthambore for…

hammira-mahakavya.s: The Hammira Mahakavya is a Sanskrit epic poem by the Jain scholar Nayachandra Suri, written in the 15th century. It recounts the history of the Chahamana (Chauhan) dynasty and especially the reign of Hammira Deva of Ranthambore and his defence of the fort against Alauddin…

habba-khatun.s: Habba Khatun was a 16th-century Kashmiri poet, remembered as the wife of Yusuf Shah Chak, one of the last sultans of Kashmir. Her songs of love and longing, many said to lament her husband's exile after the Mughal conquest of 1586, are among the best-loved works in the…

harikela.s: Harikela was an early medieval kingdom and region of south-eastern Bengal, around Chittagong and parts of Comilla and Sylhet in modern Bangladesh. It is known from inscriptions, coins and Chinese pilgrims' accounts from the 7th century, and the Chandra dynasty rose there in…

hesse.s: Hesse is a region and federal state of central Germany, with Wiesbaden as its capital and Frankfurt as its largest city. In Roman times it was the land of the Chatti, from whom the name of the Hessians is probably derived.

hemachandra.s: Hemachandra was a Jain monk, poet and polymath at the court of the Chaulukya kings Jayasimha Siddharaja and Kumarapala of Gujarat. He wrote grammars of Sanskrit and Prakrit, lexicons, works on poetics, the Trishashti-shalaka-purusha-charitra on Jain sacred history and the…

huguang.s: Huguang was a province of China under the Yuan and Ming dynasties, covering the middle Yangtze lands of present-day Hubei and Hunan and, under the Yuan, also Guangxi and Hainan. The Qing split it into Hubei and Hunan in the 17th century, but the two provinces continued to…

harz.s: The Harz is the highest mountain range of northern Germany, spread across Lower Saxony, Saxony-Anhalt and Thuringia, with the Brocken (1,141 metres) as its highest peak. Its silver, copper and lead mines, worked from the Middle Ages, enriched towns such as Goslar and the…

hindoo-holiday.s: Hindoo Holiday is a memoir by J. R. Ackerley, published in 1932, based on the journal he kept in 1923 as secretary to the Maharaja of Chhatarpur, a small princely state in Bundelkhand. An ironic and often comic portrait of the Maharaja's court, its intrigues and its ruler's…

hakau.s: Hākau was ruler (aliʻi nui) of the island of Hawaiʻi around 1500, the son and heir of Līloa. Hawaiian tradition portrays him as cruel and as having mistreated his half-brother ʻUmi-a-Līloa and the priests and chiefs of his father's court. ʻUmi led a revolt with their support,…

hawaii.s: Hawaii is an archipelago in the central Pacific Ocean and, since 1959, the 50th state of the United States, with its capital at Honolulu. Settled by Polynesian voyagers probably between about 1000 and 1200 CE, its islands were ruled by rival chiefdoms until Kamehameha I united…

honolulu.s: Honolulu is the capital and largest city of the US state of Hawaii, on the south coast of Oʻahu. Its sheltered harbour made it a centre for foreign traders from the 1790s, and Kamehameha III made it the capital of the Kingdom of Hawaii in 1845. ʻIolani Palace was the seat of…

haleakala.s: Haleakalā is the massive shield volcano that forms about three-quarters of the island of Maui, Hawaii, rising to 3,055 metres. Its summit holds a huge erosional depression often called a crater, now within Haleakalā National Park.

homeridae.s: The Homeridae, "sons of Homer", were a guild or clan of rhapsodes on the Greek island of Chios who claimed descent from Homer and recited his poems. Mentioned by Pindar, Plato and later writers, they supported Chios's claim to be Homer's birthplace, and the Homeric Hymn to…

historia-tolteca-chichimeca.s: The Historia Tolteca-Chichimeca is a 16th-century Nahuatl manuscript from Cuauhtinchan in Puebla, Mexico, combining text with pictorial maps. Written around 1545–1565, it records the migrations of the Tolteca-Chichimeca from Tollan to Cholula, their seizure of the city in the…

henry-woodward-colonist.s: Henry Woodward was an English surgeon and explorer, often called the first English settler of South Carolina. Left among the local peoples by an expedition in 1666, he learned their languages, was taken by the Spanish to St. Augustine and later joined the Carolina colony at…

hatuncolla.s: Hatuncolla is a town in the Puno region of southern Peru, north-west of Lake Titicaca and near the city of Puno. Before the Inca conquest it was the capital of the Colla kingdom, and the Incas kept it as an important provincial administrative centre.

herbert-macaulay.s: Herbert Macaulay was a Nigerian engineer, journalist and politician, often regarded as the founder of Nigerian nationalism. A grandson of Bishop Samuel Ajayi Crowther, he campaigned against British colonial policies in Lagos, founded the Nigerian National Democratic Party in…

holetown.s: Holetown is a town on the west coast of Barbados in the parish of Saint James. English settlers landed there in February 1627 aboard the William and John, sent by the merchant William Courteen, and founded the first settlement on the island, first named Jamestown.

horatio-nelson.s: Horatio Nelson was a British admiral, the most celebrated naval commander of the Revolutionary and Napoleonic Wars. While serving in the West Indies in the 1780s, he married Frances Nisbet on Nevis in 1787.

halifax-nova-scotia.s: Halifax is the capital of Nova Scotia, Canada, on one of the world's largest natural harbours. Edward Cornwallis founded it in 1749 as a British naval and military base to counter French Louisbourg, and it became the colony's capital.

hobart.s: Hobart is the capital of Tasmania, Australia, on the estuary of the Derwent River beneath Mount Wellington. Founded in 1804 by David Collins as a British penal settlement, it is Australia's second-oldest capital city after Sydney.

hurricane-david.s: Hurricane David was a Category 5 Atlantic hurricane that struck Dominica on 29 August 1979 and then the Dominican Republic and the south-eastern United States. On Dominica it destroyed most homes and the banana crop and left much of the population homeless.

harare.s: Harare is the capital and largest city of Zimbabwe. It began as Fort Salisbury, where the British South Africa Company's Pioneer Column raised the flag in September 1890, and grew into the capital of Southern Rhodesia, the Federation of Rhodesia and Nyasaland and Rhodesia.

hartford-connecticut.s: Hartford is the capital of the US state of Connecticut, on the Connecticut River. It was founded in 1636 by Puritans led by Thomas Hooker, who came from Massachusetts, and with Windsor and Wethersfield it formed the Connecticut Colony, governed under the Fundamental Orders of…

hispania.s: Hispania was the Roman name for the Iberian Peninsula, conquered by Rome from 218 BCE until the end of the Cantabrian Wars in 19 BCE. It was divided first into Hispania Citerior and Ulterior and later into Tarraconensis, Baetica and Lusitania.

hallaton-treasure.s: The Hallaton Treasure is a hoard of Iron Age and Roman objects found from 2000 near Hallaton in Leicestershire, England. Buried at an open-air ritual site in the decades around the Roman conquest of 43 CE, it includes more than 5,000 coins, most of them issued by the…

hasdingi.s: The Hasdingi were one of the two main branches of the Vandals, a Germanic people. In the 2nd century CE they moved towards the upper Tisza and the Carpathians, where, according to Cassius Dio, they took over the lands of the Costoboci around 171.

house-of-valois-angouleme.s: The House of Valois-Angoulême was a branch of the French royal Valois dynasty, descended from John, Count of Angoulême, a younger son of Louis I, Duke of Orléans. Its head, Francis I, succeeded his cousin Louis XII as king of France in 1515, and the line ruled France through…

hanover.s: Hanover is a city on the Leine in northern Germany and the capital of Lower Saxony. From 1636 it was the residence of the Guelph dukes of Calenberg, who became electors of Hanover in 1692 and, from 1714, kings of Great Britain.

house-of-albret.s: The House of Albret was a noble family of Gascony, named after the lordship of Albret in the Landes, which rose through marriage and royal service to become kings of Navarre. Jean d'Albret married Queen Catherine of Navarre in 1484, and the family kept Lower Navarre and Béarn…

house-of-chatillon.s: The House of Châtillon was a French noble family from Châtillon-sur-Marne in Champagne, prominent from the 11th to the 15th century. Its members held the counties of Blois, Saint-Pol and Penthièvre and included Gaucher V de Châtillon, constable of France, and Charles of Blois,…

henry-i-count-of-champagne.s: Henry I, called the Liberal, was count of Champagne from 1152 to 1181, son of Theobald II. He organised the Champagne fairs and made Troyes the administrative and cultural capital of a powerful principality.

haute-garonne.s: Haute-Garonne is a department of south-western France, in the Occitanie region, stretching from the Spanish border in the central Pyrenees along the upper Garonne to the plain around Toulouse, its prefecture. Created in 1790, it includes the historic district of Comminges,…

hunte.s: The Hunte is a river in Lower Saxony, Germany, about 190 kilometres long and a left tributary of the Weser. It rises in the hills near Osnabrück, flows through the Dümmer lake and past Diepholz and Oldenburg, and joins the Weser at Elsfleth.

habsburg-castle.s: Habsburg Castle is a medieval castle on the Wülpelsberg near Brugg in the Swiss canton of Aargau, built around 1020–1030 by Count Radbot and, according to tradition, Bishop Werner of Strasbourg. Its name, from Habichtsburg ('hawk's castle'), was taken by Radbot's descendants,…

hechingen.s: Hechingen is a town in the Zollernalb district of Baden-Württemberg, Germany, at the foot of the hill crowned by Hohenzollern Castle. It was the seat of the Swabian counts of Zollern and, from 1576, of the Hohenzollern-Hechingen line, raised to princely rank in 1623, whose…

hohenzollern-castle.s: Hohenzollern Castle is a hilltop castle on Mount Hohenzollern near Hechingen in Baden-Württemberg, the ancestral seat of the Hohenzollern dynasty that later ruled Brandenburg, Prussia and the German Empire. The first castle was destroyed by the Swabian imperial cities in 1423…

house-of-avesnes.s: The House of Avesnes was a noble family from Avesnes-sur-Helpe in Hainaut that rose through the marriage of Bouchard of Avesnes to Margaret, later Countess of Flanders. Bouchard's grandson John II became Count of Hainaut in 1280 and inherited Holland and Zeeland in 1299.

haarlem.s: Haarlem is a city in the Netherlands, capital of the province of North Holland, west of Amsterdam. Chartered in 1245, it was a residence of the counts of Holland and a centre of brewing, linen bleaching and cloth.

hook-and-cod-wars.s: The Hook and Cod wars were a series of factional conflicts in the County of Holland between about 1350 and 1490. They began in the succession dispute between Margaret of Bavaria and her son William V, with the Hooks (Hoeken) backing Margaret and the Cods (Kabeljauwen) her son.

house-of-wittelsbach.s: The House of Wittelsbach is a German dynasty that ruled Bavaria, as duchy, electorate and kingdom, from 1180 to 1918 and the Electoral Palatinate from 1214. Its members included Emperors Louis IV and Charles VII and kings of Sweden, Greece and Bohemia, and for a time it held…

house-of-welf.s: The House of Welf, or Guelph, is a European dynasty of Swabian and Bavarian origin. Its members included the dukes Henry the Proud and Henry the Lion, whose rivalry with the Hohenstaufen gave the Guelph name to a party in Italy, and Emperor Otto IV.

hugh-ii-of-jaffa.s: Hugh II of Le Puiset (c. 1106–1134) was Count of Jaffa in the Kingdom of Jerusalem and a cousin of Queen Melisende. Accused of treason against King Fulk, and rumoured to be the queen's lover, he rebelled in 1134 with help from the Egyptian garrison of Ascalon.

henry-iii-landgrave-of-hesse.s: Henry III (1440–1483), called the Rich, was Landgrave of Upper Hesse, ruling from Marburg after the division of Hesse in 1458. Through his marriage to Anna of Katzenelnbogen he inherited the wealthy County of Katzenelnbogen in 1479, with its Rhine tolls and the area around…

house-of-kyburg.s: The House of Kyburg was a comital family of the Swiss plateau, a branch of the counts of Dillingen named after Kyburg Castle near Winterthur. In 1218 they inherited much of the Zähringen lands, including Burgdorf, Thun and Fribourg, and they founded towns such as Winterthur,…

house-of-armagnac.s: The House of Armagnac was a noble family of Gascony, counts of Armagnac from the 10th century and of Rodez from 1302. Count Bernard VII led the Armagnac party in the French civil war against the Burgundians until his murder in 1418.

house-of-orange-nassau.s: The House of Orange-Nassau is the Dutch royal family, descended from the German house of Nassau, whose member William the Silent inherited the Principality of Orange in southern France in 1544. As stadtholders its princes led the Dutch Revolt and the Dutch Republic, and…

hasselt.s: Hasselt is a city in Belgium and the capital of the Flemish province of Limburg, on the Demer. A town of the County of Loon, it passed with the county to the prince-bishops of Liège in 1366 and became one of their 'good towns'.

hesbaye.s: The Hesbaye (Dutch Haspengouw) is a fertile loess plateau in eastern Belgium, between the Dyle, the Meuse and the Demer, spreading across the provinces of Liège, Limburg, Namur and Brabant. A Carolingian county in the early Middle Ages, it later lay largely within the…

henric-van-veldeke.s: Henric van Veldeke (c. 1150 – after 1184) was a poet from the County of Loon, near Maastricht, who wrote in an early Limburgish form of Dutch. His Eneasroman, a courtly adaptation of the French Roman d'Eneas completed in the 1180s for the Thuringian court, was regarded by…

herbert-i-count-of-maine.s: Herbert I (died c. 1035), known as Wakedog (Éveille-Chien), was Count of Maine from about 1015. He defended Maine against the expansion of Fulk Nerra of Anjou, and his nickname is said to come from night raids that kept the Angevins' dogs barking.

house-of-sternberg.s: The House of Sternberg (Šternberk) is an old Czech noble family, recorded from the 13th century and named after Český Šternberk Castle in central Bohemia, which it still owns. Its members included Kaspar Maria von Sternberg, a founder of the National Museum in Prague.

hamm.s: Hamm is a city in North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany, on the Lippe at the eastern edge of the Ruhr. It was founded in 1226 by Count Adolf I of the Mark as a planned town and became the chief town of the County of the Mark and a member of the Hanseatic League.

heinrich-schickhardt.s: Heinrich Schickhardt (1558–1635) was a German Renaissance architect and engineer in the service of Duke Frederick I of Württemberg. He laid out the new town of Freudenstadt on a grid plan and designed churches, palaces and mills, and worked extensively in Montbéliard, where he…

house-of-dampierre.s: The House of Dampierre was a French noble family from Dampierre in Champagne. William of Dampierre married Margaret, heiress of Flanders, and their son Guy of Dampierre bought Namur in 1263 and became Count of Flanders in 1278.

henry-the-blind.s: Henry the Blind (c. 1111–1196) was Count of Namur and of Luxembourg, ruling a large group of lands in the Ardennes and the Meuse valley. Long without an heir, he promised his inheritance to his nephew Baldwin V of Hainaut, but the late birth of his daughter Ermesinde in 1186…

herborn.s: Herborn is a small town in central Hesse, Germany, on the Dill, with a well-preserved old town of half-timbered houses. It belonged to the Ottonian counts of Nassau, and from 1584 it was home to the Herborn Academy, a leading Calvinist college founded by Count John VI of…

herborn-academy.s: The Herborn Academy (Hohe Schule Herborn) was a Calvinist college of university rank founded in 1584 by Count John VI of Nassau-Dillenburg at Herborn in Hesse. Teachers such as Caspar Olevian, Johannes Piscator and Johannes Althusius made it a centre of Reformed theology and…

henry-the-bearded.s: Henry the Bearded (c. 1165–1238) was Duke of Silesia from 1201 and, from 1232, High Duke of Poland as ruler of Kraków. With his wife Saint Hedwig he invited German settlers, founded towns under German law and endowed monasteries such as the Cistercian convent at Trzebnica, and…

house-of-brienne.s: The House of Brienne was a French noble family from Brienne-le-Château in Champagne that rose to prominence in the crusader states. John of Brienne became King of Jerusalem in 1210 and later co-emperor of the Latin Empire of Constantinople, his nephew Walter IV was Count of…

house-of-gonzaga.s: The House of Gonzaga was an Italian princely family that ruled Mantua from 1328 to 1708, first as captains, then as marquesses from 1433 and dukes from 1530. Its branches also held Montferrat, Guastalla, Novellara and, through Louis Gonzaga's marriage to Henriette of Cleves in…

harburg-swabia.s: Harburg is a small town in the Donau-Ries district of Bavaria, on the Wörnitz where it leaves the Ries basin. Its large hilltop castle, one of the best-preserved in southern Germany, came to the counts of Oettingen around 1300 and still belongs to the princes of…

harburg-hamburg.s: Harburg is a borough of Hamburg on the south bank of the Elbe, formerly an independent town. It belonged to the dukes of Brunswick-Lüneburg and, after 1814, to the Kingdom of Hanover, under which it grew as a port and later as an industrial town with rubber and oil works.

house-of-oldenburg.s: The House of Oldenburg is a European royal dynasty descended from the medieval counts of Oldenburg in north-western Germany. In 1448 Count Christian of Oldenburg was elected King of Denmark as Christian I, and his descendants ruled Denmark, Norway and, for periods, Sweden,…

house-of-sponheim.s: The House of Sponheim, also spelt Spanheim, was a medieval German noble family whose origins lay in the Rhineland. One branch moved to Carinthia, where it ruled as dukes from 1122 to 1269, while related lines held the Rhenish county of Sponheim and the Bavarian county of…

house-of-cardona.s: The House of Cardona was a Catalan noble family named after the castle and salt mountain of Cardona in central Catalonia. Viscounts from the 10th century, they became counts in 1375 and dukes in 1491, ranking among the greatest lords of the Crown of Aragon.

hug-roger-iii-of-pallars-sobira.n: Hug Roger III of Pallars Sobirà
hug-roger-iii-of-pallars-sobira.s: Hug Roger III was the last count of Pallars Sobirà in the Catalan Pyrenees. He sided with the Generalitat against John II in the Catalan civil war of 1462–1472 and later resisted Ferdinand II, who defeated him in 1487 and confiscated his county, granting it to the Cardona family.

harold-godwinson.s: Harold Godwinson was the last crowned Anglo-Saxon King of England, reigning as Harold II from January to October 1066. Son of Earl Godwin of Wessex, he was the realm's leading noble under Edward the Confessor and campaigned in Wales in 1063.

house-of-cirksena.s: The Cirksena were a family of East Frisian chieftains who united most of East Frisia in the 15th century. In 1464 Ulrich Cirksena was made imperial count, and his descendants ruled the County, later Principality, of East Frisia until the line died out in 1744, when Prussia…

henry-ii-count-of-rodez.s: Henry II was Count of Rodez in the late 13th century, ruling the comital part of the city and lands in the Rouergue. He was a patron of troubadour poetry and himself took part in poetic debates, and the poet Guiraut Riquier spent his last years at his court.

helena-kantakouzene.s: Helena Kantakouzene was a Byzantine noblewoman, granddaughter of Emperor John VI Kantakouzenos, who married Louis Fadrique, Count of Salona. After his death in 1382 she governed the county for their daughter Maria.

henry-iii-count-of-sayn.s: Henry III was Count of Sayn and the most powerful ruler of his line, governing until his death in 1247. He built up a large territory in the Westerwald and the Siegerland.

hunsruck.s: The Hunsrück is a low mountain range in Rhineland-Palatinate, bounded by the Moselle, the Rhine, the Nahe and the Saar. In the Middle Ages it was a patchwork of small lordships, among them the counties of Sponheim and Veldenz, the lands of the Wild- and Rhinegraves and the…

halle-saale.s: Halle is a city on the Saale in Saxony-Anhalt, long known for its salt springs. Ruled by the archbishops of Magdeburg until 1680, it then passed to Brandenburg-Prussia, whose new university, founded in 1694, became a centre of Pietism and the early Enlightenment.

house-of-waldburg.s: The House of Waldburg is a Swabian noble family named after Waldburg castle near Ravensburg. Its members served the Hohenstaufen emperors as imperial stewards (Truchsess) and later divided into several lines, among them Waldburg-Wolfegg and Waldburg-Zeil, which ruled small…

house-of-lowenstein-wertheim.s: The House of Löwenstein-Wertheim is a German noble family descended from Elector Frederick I of the Palatinate and his morganatic wife Clara Tott, whose son Louis became count of Löwenstein. Through marriage it inherited the County of Wertheim on the Main in the late 16th…

hugh-davranches-earl-of-chester.s: Hugh d'Avranches was a Norman nobleman, a companion of William the Conqueror, who became Earl of Chester in 1071. Ruling Cheshire with near-regal powers, he and his cousin Robert of Rhuddlan pushed into north Wales and for a time dominated Gwynedd.

haci-i-giray.s: Hacı I Giray was the founder of the Crimean Khanate and of the Giray dynasty, which ruled it until 1783. A descendant of Genghis Khan through Jochi, he established an independent khanate in Crimea around 1441 with Lithuanian support, as the Golden Horde broke apart.

house-of-trastamara.s: The House of Trastámara was a Spanish royal dynasty named after the county of Trastámara in Galicia. It came to the throne of Castile in 1369, when Henry II killed his half-brother Peter the Cruel, and to the Crown of Aragon in 1412 through the Compromise of Caspe.

hiero-i-of-syracuse.s: Hiero I was tyrant of Gela and then, from 478 BCE, of Syracuse, succeeding his brother Gelon. In 474 BCE his fleet, allied with Cumae, destroyed an Etruscan fleet off Cumae, breaking Etruscan sea power.

helmin-wiels.s: Helmin Wiels was a Curaçao politician who founded the Pueblo Soberano party, which campaigned for Curaçao's independence and against corruption. His party became the largest in parliament in the 2012 election.

hesiod.s: Hesiod was a Greek poet of around 700 BCE who lived at Ascra in Boeotia, where his father had settled after leaving Cyme in Aeolis. His Theogony describes the origins of the gods and the world, and his Works and Days gives advice on farming, work and justice.

hyrcania.s: Hyrcania was a historical region south-east of the Caspian Sea, in the modern Iranian provinces of Golestan and Mazandaran and parts of Turkmenistan. A fertile, forested province of the Achaemenid, Seleucid and Parthian empires, it bordered the steppe of nomadic peoples such…

hohhot.s: Hohhot is the capital of the Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region of China, on the plain north of the great bend of the Yellow River. The area was an early centre of the Tuoba Xianbei, and the city was founded in the 1570s by the Tumed ruler Altan Khan, receiving the Chinese name…

horinger.s: Horinger is a county of Hohhot in Inner Mongolia, China, south of the city. It contains the ruins of Shengle, the early capital of the Tuoba Xianbei, and an Eastern Han tomb whose wall paintings show official life and farming on the northern frontier of China in the 2nd century.

heinrich-plutschau.s: Heinrich Plütschau was a German Lutheran missionary who, with Bartholomäus Ziegenbalg, founded the Tranquebar Mission in Danish India in 1706, the first Protestant mission in India. Sent by King Frederick IV of Denmark, he worked there until 1711, then returned to Europe and…

harjedalen.s: Härjedalen is a mountainous province in central Sweden, bordering Norway. Long ruled from Norway, it passed with Jämtland to Sweden under the Treaty of Brömsebro in 1645, which ended the Torstenson War.

herzegovina.s: Herzegovina is the southern region of Bosnia and Herzegovina, centred on the Neretva valley and the city of Mostar. In the Middle Ages it formed the principality of Hum (Zachlumia), and it takes its name from the title herceg, duke, used by the nobleman Stjepan Vukčić Kosača…

hoshiarpur-district.s: Hoshiarpur district lies in the Indian state of Punjab, between the Beas and the Sutlej at the foot of the Shivalik hills, with its headquarters at the city of Hoshiarpur. It formed part of the Jalandhar Doab, which Britain annexed from the Sikh kingdom in 1846.

hippos.s: Hippos was a Hellenistic and Roman city of the Decapolis on a flat-topped hill east of the Sea of Galilee, in the modern Golan region of Israel. Founded in the 2nd century BCE, it prospered as a Greek-speaking city with temples, a forum and, later, several churches.

halkyn-mountain.s: Halkyn Mountain is a limestone upland in Flintshire, north-east Wales, rich in veins of lead ore. The ore was mined from Roman times, when inscribed lead pigs from the area name the local Deceangli, until the 20th century, and the hill is scarred by old shafts and spoil heaps.

helena-of-bulgaria-empress-of-serbia.n: Helena of Bulgaria, Empress of Serbia
helena-of-bulgaria-empress-of-serbia.s: Helena of Bulgaria, called Jelena in Serbian, was the wife of Stefan Dušan and empress of Serbia. A sister of the Bulgarian tsar Ivan Alexander, she married Dušan in 1332 and took part in government.

hexamilion-wall.s: The Hexamilion was a defensive wall about six Roman miles long across the Isthmus of Corinth, guarding the only land route into the Peloponnese. It was built in the early 5th century CE under Theodosius II and repaired several times.

hamgyong-province.s: Hamgyong was one of the eight provinces of Joseon Korea, on the north-east coast of the peninsula bordering Manchuria. Mountainous and long a frontier against the Jurchen, it was split in 1896 into North and South Hamgyong, which are now provinces of North Korea.

hugo-junkers.s: Hugo Junkers was a German engineer and industrialist who pioneered all-metal aircraft. Starting with gas appliances at Dessau in the 1890s, he built the Junkers J 1, the first practical all-metal aeroplane, in 1915 and the F 13 airliner in 1919.

humphrey-of-hauteville.s: Humphrey of Hauteville was count of the Normans of Apulia from 1051 to 1057, succeeding his murdered brother Drogo. In 1053 he was among the leaders of the Norman army that defeated and captured Pope Leo IX at the Battle of Civitate.

house-of-ligne.s: The House of Ligne is a noble family of Hainaut, in present-day Belgium, named after the village of Ligne near Ath and recorded from the 11th century. Its members served the Habsburgs as soldiers and diplomats, and in the 16th century a branch inherited the lordship of…

hedwig-jagiellon-duchess-of-bavaria.s: Hedwig Jagiellon was a Polish princess, a daughter of King Casimir IV, who married Duke George the Rich of Bavaria-Landshut in 1475. Their wedding at Landshut was one of the most lavish festivities of the late Middle Ages and is re-enacted every four years as the Landshut…

holocaust.s: The Holocaust was the genocide of about six million European Jews by Nazi Germany and its collaborators during the Second World War. From 1941 mass shootings in the occupied Soviet territories and the Baltic states were followed by deportations to extermination camps such as…

house-of-varano.s: The Varano were a noble family who ruled Camerino in the Marche from the second half of the 13th century until 1539. Gentile da Varano led the city from 1262, and his descendants served as papal vicars and condottieri.

house-of-eppenstein.s: The Eppensteiners were a noble family from Styria who held the Duchy of Carinthia, together with the March of Verona, for long periods between 1011 and 1122. Adalbero of Eppenstein became duke in 1011 but was deposed by Emperor Conrad II in 1035; his descendants regained the…

henry-ii-duke-of-bavaria.s: Henry the Quarrelsome was Duke of Bavaria from 955 to 976 and again from 985 to 995, a member of the Ottonian dynasty and cousin of Emperor Otto II. His repeated rebellions led Otto to depose him and to split off Carinthia as a separate duchy in 976, and after Otto's death in…

house-of-andechs.s: The counts of Andechs were a Bavarian noble family named after their castle above the Ammersee. In 1180 they took the title of dukes of Merania, and they held wide lands in Bavaria, Franconia, Tyrol, Istria and Carniola.

harju-county.s: Harju County is a county in northern Estonia that includes the capital, Tallinn. The historic land of Harjumaa, known in German as Harrien, was conquered by Denmark in 1219, and its German vassals formed the knighthood of Harrien, which in 1561 submitted to Sweden together…

house-of-babenberg.s: The House of Babenberg ruled Austria from 976, first as margraves and from 1156 as dukes, after the Privilegium Minus raised the march to a duchy. Leopold I was the first margrave, and his descendants moved their seat to Vienna and acquired Styria in 1192.

hrodgaud.s: Hrodgaud was the last Lombard Duke of Friuli. After Charlemagne conquered the Lombard Kingdom in 774 he kept his duchy, but in 776 he rebelled, hoping to restore Lombard rule with the help of other dukes.

house-of-liechtenstein.s: The House of Liechtenstein is an Austrian noble family that takes its name from Liechtenstein Castle near Mödling, south of Vienna. Rising in Habsburg service, its members acquired large estates in Moravia, Bohemia and Silesia, including the Duchy of Krnov in the 1620s.

house-of-guise.s: The House of Guise was a French ducal family, a junior branch of the House of Lorraine founded by Claude of Lorraine, who was made Duke of Guise in 1528. Its leaders, among them Francis, Duke of Guise, and his son Henry, headed the Catholic party and the Catholic League in the…

house-of-gonzaga-nevers.s: Gonzaga-Nevers was a branch of the Gonzaga family descended from Louis Gonzaga, who became Duke of Nevers in France by marriage in 1565. When the main line died out in 1627, his son Charles I Gonzaga-Nevers inherited Mantua and Montferrat, provoking the War of the Mantuan…

house-of-cybo-malaspina.s: Cybo-Malaspina was a noble family formed when Lorenzo Cybo, a grandson of Pope Innocent VIII, married Ricciarda Malaspina, heiress of Massa and Carrara, in 1520. Their son Alberico I took the combined name and was made prince in 1568, and the family ruled Massa and Carrara as…

house-of-mecklenburg.s: The House of Mecklenburg, also called the Niklotings, was a dynasty descended from Niklot, a prince of the Slavic Obotrites who died fighting the Saxons in 1160. His son Pribislav accepted Christianity and became a vassal of Henry the Lion, and the family ruled Mecklenburg as…

house-of-pico.s: The Pico were an Italian noble family who ruled Mirandola, north of Modena, from the 14th century until 1708, first as imperial vicars and lords and later as princes and dukes. The humanist Giovanni Pico della Mirandola was a member of the family.

house-of-plantagenet.s: The House of Plantagenet was a royal dynasty descended from Geoffrey Plantagenet, Count of Anjou, whose son became King Henry II of England in 1154. Through inheritance and marriage Henry ruled England, Normandy, Anjou and Aquitaine, the so-called Angevin Empire, though his…

house-of-podebrady.s: The Poděbrady were a Bohemian noble family named after their castle at Poděbrady on the Elbe, whose most famous member was George of Poděbrady, King of Bohemia from 1458 to 1471. His sons became dukes of Münsterberg (Ziębice) and held Silesian duchies including Oleśnica and,…

house-of-vasa.s: The House of Vasa was a Swedish royal dynasty founded by Gustav I, who became King of Sweden in 1523. Through Sigismund III, elected King of Poland in 1587, a Polish branch ruled the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth until the abdication of John II Casimir in 1668.
