hippodamus-of-miletus.s: Hippodamus of Miletus was a Greek architect and political thinker of the 5th century BCE, regarded in antiquity as the father of town planning. His name became attached to the grid plan of straight streets crossing at right angles, used in the rebuilding of Miletus after 479 BCE.

histiaeus.s: Histiaeus was the tyrant of Miletus under the Persian king Darius I in the late 6th century BCE. According to Herodotus he guarded Darius's bridge over the Danube during the Scythian campaign and was later kept at the Persian court, from where he encouraged his deputy and…

harry-shepard-knapp.s: Harry Shepard Knapp was an officer of the United States Navy who proclaimed the American military government of the Dominican Republic in November 1916, after the Dominican congress refused American demands for control of the country's finances and army. He served as military…

hughes-peynado-plan.s: The Hughes–Peynado plan was the 1922 agreement between the American secretary of state Charles Evans Hughes and the Dominican lawyer Francisco Peynado that set the terms for ending the United States occupation of the Dominican Republic. It provided for a provisional Dominican…

hosokawa-harumoto.s: Hosokawa Harumoto was a Japanese warlord who served as kanrei, deputy to the Ashikaga shogun, and dominated Kyoto in the 1530s and 1540s. His power rested on his retainers, above all the Miyoshi, but in 1549 Miyoshi Nagayoshi turned against him and defeated his forces at…

huaca-de-la-luna.s: The Huaca de la Luna, 'Temple of the Moon', is a great adobe temple at the Moche capital of Huacas de Moche, near Trujillo on the north coast of Peru. Rebuilt in successive layers between about 100 and 800 CE, it served as a religious centre where human sacrifice took place.

huaca-del-sol.s: The Huaca del Sol, 'Temple of the Sun', is a vast stepped platform of mud brick at Huacas de Moche near Trujillo, Peru, built by the Moche culture between about 100 and 800 CE. Made of an estimated hundred million adobe bricks, many bearing makers' marks, it was one of the…

huacas-de-moche.s: Huacas de Moche is the archaeological site of the capital of the Moche culture, in the Moche valley just south of Trujillo on the north coast of Peru. Between the great platform of the Huaca del Sol and the painted temple of the Huaca de la Luna lay an urban zone of houses,…

hpakant.s: Hpakant is a town in Kachin State in northern Myanmar, at the centre of the world's largest deposits of high-quality jadeite. Jade from the area was traded to China from at least the 18th century, through the Shan state of Mogaung.

haw-wars.s: The Haw wars were raids and campaigns between about 1865 and 1890 by bands of Chinese irregulars, called Haw, who had fled southern China after the Taiping and related rebellions. They ravaged Muang Phuan, Luang Prabang and other Lao and Tai lands.

hoveyzeh.s: Hoveyzeh is a town in Khuzestan province in south-western Iran, near the marshes on the Iraqi border. From the 15th century it was the capital of the Musha'sha, a dynasty of Arab sayyids who ruled much of Khuzestan under Safavid overlordship.

hafez.s: Hafez was a Persian poet of Shiraz, the most celebrated master of the ghazal, or lyric love poem. He lived under the Injuid and Muzaffarid rulers of Fars, praising some patrons and mocking the piety of others.

helen-of-troy.s: In Greek mythology, Helen was the daughter of Zeus and Leda and the wife of Menelaus, king of Sparta. Her abduction or flight with the Trojan prince Paris caused the Trojan War, told in the Homeric epics.

hunza-nagar-campaign.s: The Hunza-Nagar Campaign was a British expedition of December 1891 led by Colonel Algernon Durand against the states of Hunza and Nagar in the Karakoram. After the storming of the fort of Nilt, in which three Victoria Crosses were won, both states submitted and came under the…

helmand-river.s: The Helmand is the longest river in Afghanistan, flowing about 1,150 km from the Hindu Kush south-west through desert to the Sistan basin on the Iranian border. Its waters feed the inland delta and lakes of Sistan, where irrigation supported cities and kingdoms from antiquity,…

hiram-bingham-iii.s: Hiram Bingham III was an American academic, explorer and politician who in 1911 led the Yale expedition that brought Machu Picchu to international attention. On the same journey he visited Vitcos and Espíritu Pampa in search of Vilcabamba, the last Inca refuge.

henry-hudson.s: Henry Hudson was an English navigator who searched for a northern sea route to Asia. Sailing for the Dutch East India Company in the Half Moon in 1609, he explored the river now named after him, opening the way for the Dutch fur trade and New Netherland.

hemavathi.s: Hemavathi is a village in southern Andhra Pradesh, India, near the border with Karnataka, known in medieval inscriptions as Henjeru. It was the main capital of the Nolamba dynasty in the 9th and 10th centuries.

hvalsey-church.s: Hvalsey Church is a ruined stone church of the Norse Eastern Settlement in southern Greenland, near modern Qaqortoq, and the best-preserved Norse building in Greenland. A wedding held there in September 1408, recorded in Icelandic documents, is the last written record of the…

hiraizumi.s: Hiraizumi is a town in Iwate prefecture in northern Honshu, Japan. In the 12th century it was the seat of the Northern Fujiwara, who ruled Mutsu and Dewa and, with gold from the region, made it a rich cultural centre rivalling Kyoto.

hulu-guang.s: Hulü Guang was one of the leading generals of the Northern Qi dynasty in northern China, repeatedly defeating the rival Northern Zhou. The son of the general Hulü Jin, he became chancellor, and his daughter married the emperor Gao Wei.

harry-nkumbula.s: Harry Nkumbula was a Zambian nationalist who led the Northern Rhodesia African National Congress from 1951 and campaigned against the Federation of Rhodesia and Nyasaland. Kenneth Kaunda and other younger leaders broke away from him in 1958, and their movement soon became the…

huancayo.s: Huancayo is a city in the central highlands of Peru, capital of the Junín region, in the Mantaro valley at about 3,250 m. A Spanish town founded in the 16th century, it was where a congress adopted the Huancayo Constitution of 1839, and where Ramón Castilla decreed the…

harold-harefoot.s: Harold Harefoot was king of England from 1035 to 1040, the son of Cnut the Great and his first wife, Ælfgifu of Northampton. When Cnut died in 1035 his heir Harthacnut was held back in Denmark, and Harold acted first as regent and from 1037 as king.

harthacnut.s: Harthacnut was king of Denmark from 1035 and of England from 1040 to 1042, the son of Cnut the Great and Emma of Normandy. Kept in Denmark by the threat of Magnus the Good of Norway, he lost England for a time to his half-brother Harold Harefoot but took the throne after…

hell-ville.s: Hell-Ville, officially Andoany, is the main town of the island of Nosy Be off north-western Madagascar. It was named after Admiral Anne Chrétien Louis de Hell, governor of Bourbon (Réunion), under whom France took possession of Nosy Be in 1841.

herculaneum.s: Herculaneum was an ancient Roman town on the Bay of Naples, at modern Ercolano, buried by the eruption of Mount Vesuvius in 79 CE. Covered by deep volcanic deposits, it preserved wooden structures, food and, in the Villa of the Papyri, a library of carbonised scrolls.

hidalgo-del-parral.s: Hidalgo del Parral, usually called Parral, is a city in southern Chihuahua, Mexico. It grew after rich silver deposits were found in 1631 and for much of the 17th century was the residence of the governors of Nueva Vizcaya and one of the leading mining towns of New Spain.

hiempsal-i.s: Hiempsal I was a Numidian prince, the younger son of King Micipsa, who inherited a share of the kingdom with his brother Adherbal and his cousin Jugurtha in 118 BCE. Quarrels over the division began almost at once, and Jugurtha had him murdered soon afterwards.

honno-ji.s: Honnō-ji is a Buddhist temple of the Hokke (Nichiren) school in Kyoto. On 21 June 1582 Oda Nobunaga, lodging there with few guards, was attacked by his general Akechi Mitsuhide and died as the temple burned, an event known as the Honnō-ji Incident.

hakone-checkpoint.s: The Hakone Checkpoint was a barrier station on the Tōkaidō highway beside Lake Ashi in the Hakone mountains, set up by the Tokugawa shogunate in 1619. Guards inspected travellers between Edo and the western provinces, watching above all for guns entering and women leaving Edo,…

henry-douglas-warden.s: Henry Douglas Warden was a British army officer who served as British Resident in the territory between the Orange and Vaal rivers. In 1846 he founded Bloemfontein as his headquarters, and from 1848 he administered the Orange River Sovereignty with few troops and little money.

herero-people.s: The Herero are a Bantu-speaking, cattle-herding people of central and northern Namibia and neighbouring Botswana. In the 19th century they contested land and herds with the Oorlam and Nama, and under Maharero won their independence from Jonker Afrikaner's successors in the 1860s.

hakata.s: Hakata is a historic port on Hakata Bay in northern Kyushu, now a ward of the city of Fukuoka. For centuries it was Japan's main gateway for trade with China and Korea, and the Mongol invasions of 1274 and 1281 landed nearby.

hikayat-aceh.s: The Hikayat Aceh is a Malay court chronicle of the Aceh Sultanate, written in the 17th century in praise of Sultan Iskandar Muda. It tells of his ancestry, birth and youth in a style influenced by Persian royal biographies, and survives only incompletely.

hikayat-prang-sabi.s: The Hikayat Prang Sabi, 'Tale of the Holy War', is an Acehnese epic poem calling believers to fight the unbelievers and promising the rewards of martyrdom. Its best-known version was composed in the 1880s, during the Aceh War against the Dutch, and is attributed to Teungku…

hieronymus-of-cardia.s: Hieronymus of Cardia was a Greek general, statesman and historian who served Eumenes and then the Antigonid kings Antigonus I, Demetrius Poliorcetes and Antigonus II Gonatas. His history of the Successors of Alexander the Great, from 323 BCE to at least the death of Pyrrhus in…

hipolito-yrigoyen.s: Hipólito Yrigoyen was the leader of the Radical Civic Union and the first Argentine president elected under the secret and compulsory male suffrage of the Sáenz Peña Law, serving from 1916 to 1922 and again from 1928. Popular with the middle classes, he was overthrown on 6…

hormuzd-rassam.s: Hormuzd Rassam was an Assyriologist and diplomat, born in Mosul to an Assyrian Christian family, who worked as Austen Henry Layard's assistant and later excavated for the British Museum. In 1853 he found the North Palace of Ashurbanipal at Nineveh with much of its library and…

hans-kudlich.s: Hans Kudlich was a Silesian-born Austrian politician, the youngest deputy in the Austrian Reichstag of 1848, whose motion of July that year led to the abolition of the labour services and other obligations of peasants to their landlords. After the revolution's defeat he fled…

holy-alliance.s: The Holy Alliance was an agreement signed in September 1815 by the rulers of Russia, Austria and Prussia, proposed by Tsar Alexander I, by which they pledged to govern according to Christian principles. Under Metternich's influence it came to stand for the conservative powers'…

humayun-shah-bahmani.s: Humayun Shah was sultan of the Bahmani Sultanate from 1458 to 1461, the son of Ala-ud-Din Ahmad Shah. He appointed Mahmud Gawan as a leading minister, but his short reign was remembered for harsh punishment of rebels and rivals, which earned him the name "the Cruel" in later…

heilongjiang.s: Heilongjiang is the northernmost province of China, in north-east Manchuria, bordering Russia along the Amur, whose Chinese name it bears. Its capital is Harbin.

heishui-mohe.s: The Heishui Mohe, or Black Water Mohe, were the northernmost group of the Mohe peoples, living along the Amur River in Manchuria. They resisted absorption by Balhae, and their submission to Tang protection in the 720s led to war between Balhae and Tang.

haliartus.s: Haliartus was an ancient city of Boeotia on the southern shore of Lake Copais and a member of the Boeotian League. In 395 BCE the Spartan commander Lysander was killed beneath its walls at the start of the Corinthian War.

herbert-baker.s: Sir Herbert Baker was an English architect who worked mainly in South Africa and India. In South Africa he designed the Union Buildings in Pretoria, and in New Delhi he worked with Edwin Lutyens, designing the two Secretariat buildings and the circular Parliament House.

hasanwayhids.s: The Hasanwayhids were a Kurdish dynasty that ruled parts of the central Zagros, including Dinawar and Kermanshah, from about 959 to 1015. Founded by Hasanwayh ibn Husayn, chief of the Barzikani Kurds, it reached its height under his son Badr ibn Hasanwayh, who was recognised…

hathor.s: Hathor was one of the principal goddesses of ancient Egypt, associated with the sky, love, music, motherhood and foreign lands, and often shown as a cow or a woman with cow horns and a sun disc. Her main cult centre was Dendera.

hecate.s: Hecate was a Greek goddess associated with crossroads, entrances, night, magic and the moon, often shown with torches or in triple form. She was widely worshipped, and Byzantium honoured her as a protector of the city.

hieronymus-wolf.s: Hieronymus Wolf was a German humanist scholar and librarian in Augsburg who edited and translated Greek authors. His Corpus Historiae Byzantinae of 1557, a collection of medieval Greek historians, did much to popularise the term 'Byzantine' for the Eastern Roman Empire, whose…

hasdai-ibn-shaprut.s: Hasdai ibn Shaprut was a Jewish physician, diplomat and patron at the court of the caliphs Abd al-Rahman III and al-Hakam II in Córdoba. He received foreign embassies, helped prepare an Arabic version of Dioscorides' De materia medica and treated King Sancho I of León.

harold-innis.s: Harold Innis was a Canadian economic historian at the University of Toronto. In works such as The Fur Trade in Canada he developed the staples thesis, which explained Canada's development through the export of raw materials such as fur, fish, timber and wheat.

heinrich-bullinger.s: Heinrich Bullinger was a Swiss Reformer who succeeded Huldrych Zwingli as head of the Zürich church in 1531 and led it until his death. Through a vast correspondence he advised Reformed churches across Europe.

history-of-the-country-of-albania.n: History of the Country of Albania
history-of-the-country-of-albania.s: The History of the Country of Albania is an Armenian-language history of Caucasian Albania attributed to Movses Kaghankatvatsi, probably compiled in the tenth century from older material. In three books it covers the country from its legendary origins through its kings, its…

hippocrates-of-chios.s: Hippocrates of Chios was a Greek mathematician who worked in Athens in the fifth century BCE. He wrote the first known systematic Elements of geometry, a forerunner of Euclid's, and is famous for showing that certain figures bounded by circular arcs, the lunes, have areas…

h-v-evatt.s: H. V. Evatt was an Australian judge and Labor politician. He served on the High Court and then as minister for external affairs from 1941 to 1949, playing a prominent part in founding the United Nations.

harvester-case.s: The Harvester case of 1907 was a decision of Justice H. B. Higgins of the Australian Commonwealth Court of Conciliation and Arbitration concerning H. V. McKay's Sunshine Harvester works in Melbourne. Higgins ruled that a fair and reasonable wage must meet the needs of a…

howard-florey.s: Howard Florey was an Australian pathologist, born in Adelaide, who led the team at Oxford that turned penicillin into a usable medicine. With Ernst Chain and others he purified the drug and showed its power against bacterial infection in 1940 and 1941, and its mass production…

house-of-commons-of-the-united-kingdom.n: House of Commons of the United Kingdom
house-of-commons-of-the-united-kingdom.s: The House of Commons is the elected lower house of the Parliament of the United Kingdom, meeting in the Palace of Westminster, to which the government is responsible. Its members are chosen by constituencies, and its control of taxation and supply made it the dominant chamber.

heart-of-darkness.s: Heart of Darkness is a novella by Joseph Conrad, published in serial form in 1899 and as a book in 1902. Narrated by the seaman Marlow, it describes a journey up an African river to the ivory agent Kurtz, drawing on Conrad's own voyage up the Congo in 1890.

huis-ter-beurze.s: Huis ter Beurze is a medieval house in Bruges that belonged to the Van der Beurse family of innkeepers and brokers. Italian and other foreign merchants met on the square in front of it to trade bills of exchange and goods, and their gatherings gave the family's name to the…

haine.s: The Haine is a river in the Belgian province of Hainaut and the French Nord department, a tributary of the Scheldt. It flows west past Mons and through the Borinage coalfield to join the Scheldt at Condé-sur-l'Escaut.

haigerloch.s: Haigerloch is a small town on the Eyach in the Zollernalb district of Baden-Württemberg, Germany. The lordship of Haigerloch passed to the counts of Zollern in 1497 in exchange for Rhäzüns and was the seat of a separate line of counts after the division of 1576.

house-of-trencavel.s: The Trencavel were a family of viscounts in Languedoc who in the eleventh and twelfth centuries held Albi, Béziers, Carcassonne, Nîmes and Agde, shifting allegiance between the counts of Toulouse and Barcelona. Accused of protecting Cathars, Viscount Raymond-Roger Trencavel…

henry-ii-of-castile.s: Henry II was king of Castile from 1369 to 1379, an illegitimate son of Alfonso XI. He led a civil war against his half-brother Peter I with French and Aragonese support, was defeated at Nájera in 1367, and killed Peter after the Battle of Montiel in 1369.

hippodrome-of-constantinople.s: The Hippodrome of Constantinople was the chariot-racing stadium of the Byzantine capital, begun under Septimius Severus and enlarged by Constantine the Great. It was the centre of the city's public life and of the Blue and Green factions, and the Nika riots of 532 began there.

hyde-parker.s: Sir Hyde Parker was a British admiral who commanded the fleet sent in 1801 to break the League of Armed Neutrality. At the Battle of Copenhagen his signal to break off the action was famously ignored by his second-in-command, Horatio Nelson, who went on to defeat the Danish…

house-of-luxembourg.s: The House of Luxembourg was a dynasty of counts of Luxembourg that rose to the first rank of European royalty in the fourteenth century. It produced the emperors Henry VII, Charles IV and Sigismund, ruled Bohemia from 1310 and Hungary from 1387, and held Brandenburg from 1373.

hadewijch.s: Hadewijch was a Brabantine mystic and poet of the thirteenth century, probably a beguine living in or near Antwerp or Brussels. Her visions, letters and poems in Middle Dutch describe the soul's love for God in the language of courtly love, minne.

house-of-dreux.s: The House of Dreux was a cadet branch of the French royal Capetian dynasty, descended from Robert I, Count of Dreux, a son of Louis VI. In 1213 Philip II married the Breton heiress Alix to Peter Mauclerc of Dreux, whose descendants, including the later Montfort dukes, ruled…

henry-i-duke-of-burgundy.s: Henry I, known as Henry the Great, was duke of Burgundy from 965 to 1002, a son of Hugh the Great and brother of Hugh Capet. He died without a legitimate son, having adopted his stepson Otto-William, and his nephew King Robert II of France fought a long war to secure the duchy…

hospices-de-beaune.s: The Hospices de Beaune is a former charitable hospital in Beaune, Burgundy, founded in 1443 by Nicolas Rolin, chancellor of Philip the Good, and his wife Guigone de Salins. Its Hôtel-Dieu, with a roof of glazed coloured tiles, is a masterpiece of late Gothic architecture, and…

hugh-iii-duke-of-burgundy.s: Hugh III was duke of Burgundy from 1162 to 1192. He took part in the Third Crusade and, when Philip II of France returned home in 1191, commanded the French contingent alongside Richard the Lionheart, fighting at Arsuf.

hugh-iv-duke-of-burgundy.s: Hugh IV was duke of Burgundy from 1218 to 1272. He acquired the county of Chalon in 1237, extending the duchy, took part in the Barons' Crusade of 1239 and joined Louis IX's crusade to Egypt in 1248–1250.

house-of-habsburg-lorraine.s: The House of Habsburg-Lorraine was the dynasty founded by the marriage in 1736 of Maria Theresa, heiress of the Habsburg lands, and Francis Stephen, duke of Lorraine, later Emperor Francis I. Its members ruled the Habsburg Monarchy, then the Austrian Empire and…

house-of-medici.s: The House of Medici was a Florentine banking family that dominated Florence from 1434, when Cosimo the Elder returned from exile. Its members included Lorenzo the Magnificent and the popes Leo X and Clement VII, and from 1532 they ruled as dukes of Florence and from 1569 as…

house-of-hauteville.s: The House of Hauteville was a Norman family from Hauteville-la-Guichard in the Cotentin whose sons won lands in southern Italy from the 1030s. Robert Guiscard became duke of Apulia and Calabria, his brother Roger I conquered Sicily between 1061 and 1091, and Roger II united…

herluin.s: Herluin was a Norman knight who gave up military life to become a monk and founded the abbey of Bec in Normandy around 1034, serving as its first abbot. Under him Lanfranc of Pavia, and later Anselm, made Bec one of the leading schools of Europe.

heinrich-rubenow.s: Heinrich Rubenow was a lawyer and burgomaster of Greifswald in Pomerania who founded the University of Greifswald in 1456 with the support of Duke Wartislaw IX and papal approval, and served as its first rector. One of the oldest universities of northern Europe, it trained…

haute-savoie.s: Haute-Savoie is a department of south-eastern France, bordering Switzerland and Italy, with Annecy as its prefecture. It covers the northern part of the former Duchy of Savoy, including the Chablais, the Genevois and the Mont Blanc massif.

harzburg.s: The Harzburg was a royal castle built by Emperor Henry IV from about 1065 on a hill above present-day Bad Harzburg in the Harz mountains. It was the chief of a ring of fortresses that the Saxon nobility saw as instruments of royal oppression, and in 1074, during the Saxon…

henry-the-proud.s: Henry the Proud was a Welf prince who was Duke of Bavaria from 1126 and Duke of Saxony from 1137. Son-in-law and heir of Emperor Lothair III, he expected to succeed him in 1138, but the princes elected Conrad III, who took both duchies from him.

hnlms-de-zeven-provincien-1910.s: De Zeven Provinciën was a Dutch coastal defence ship launched in 1909 and stationed in the East Indies. In February 1933 Indonesian and Dutch sailors seized it off Sumatra in protest against pay cuts; after several days a naval aircraft bombed the ship, killing 23 men, and the…

herman-boerhaave.s: Herman Boerhaave was a Dutch physician, chemist and botanist who taught at Leiden University from 1701. He brought students to the bedside and is regarded as a founder of clinical teaching, and his textbooks of medicine and chemistry were used across Europe.

hms-royal-charles-1655.s: The Royal Charles was an English warship of about eighty guns, launched in 1655 as the Naseby for Oliver Cromwell's navy and renamed at the Restoration in 1660, when it carried Charles II home from the Netherlands. During the Raid on the Medway in June 1667, Dutch forces under…

han-zhao.s: Han Zhao was a state of northern China founded in 304 by Liu Yuan, a Xiongnu leader, at the start of the Sixteen Kingdoms period. Calling his state Han to claim the legacy of the Han dynasty, he and his son Liu Cong destroyed the Western Jin, sacking Luoyang in 311 and taking…

herihor.s: Herihor was an Egyptian army officer who became High Priest of Amun at Thebes around 1080 BCE, in the last years of Ramesses XI and the Twentieth Dynasty. Combining military command, the post of viceroy of Kush and the high priesthood, he ruled Upper Egypt in practice, and in…

heidelberg-castle.s: Heidelberg Castle is the ruined residence of the electors palatine above the Neckar in Heidelberg, Germany. Built and extended from the thirteenth century, it gained Renaissance palaces such as the Ottheinrich Building, but French troops blew up much of it in 1689 and 1693…

henry-v-count-palatine-of-the-rhine.n: Henry V, Count Palatine of the Rhine
henry-v-count-palatine-of-the-rhine.s: Henry of Brunswick, the eldest son of Henry the Lion, became count palatine of the Rhine in 1195 through his marriage to Agnes, heiress of Conrad of Hohenstaufen. A brother of Emperor Otto IV, he took part in the Welf struggle for the German throne.

heinrich-von-bruhl.s: Count Heinrich von Brühl was the leading minister of Saxony under Augustus III, Elector of Saxony and King of Poland, from the late 1730s until 1763. He controlled finance and patronage and promoted the arts, but his extravagance left the state heavily in debt, and Saxony was…

hall-of-the-ambassadors-alhambra.s: The Hall of the Ambassadors (Salón de Embajadores) is the largest room of the Nasrid palaces of the Alhambra in Granada, inside the Comares Tower, and served as the throne room of the emirs. Built under Yusuf I in the fourteenth century, it has a carved wooden dome of…

herostratus.s: Herostratus was a man of Ephesus who in 356 BCE set fire to the Temple of Artemis, traditionally on the night Alexander the Great was born, in order to win lasting fame. The Ephesians executed him and forbade anyone to mention his name, but the historian Theopompus recorded it.

hipponax.s: Hipponax of Ephesus was a Greek iambic poet of the sixth century BCE who was expelled from Ephesus by its tyrants and lived at Clazomenae. His abusive, comic verse about beggars, thieves and his enemies, written in a mixed Ionic dialect, used the limping iambic metre…

hammaburg.s: The Hammaburg was a fortification built in the early 9th century near the meeting of the Alster and the Elbe, from which Hamburg takes its name. Probably founded under Charlemagne or Louis the Pious to secure the Frankish frontier in Saxony, it became the seat of Archbishop…

hamburg-dramaturgy.s: The Hamburg Dramaturgy is a collection of essays by Gotthold Ephraim Lessing, published in 1767–1769 as reviews for Hamburg's short-lived German National Theatre. Discussing the plays performed there, Lessing criticised the dominance of French classical drama, reinterpreted…

hamburg-stock-exchange.s: The Hamburg Stock Exchange, founded in 1558, is the oldest exchange in Germany. It began as a meeting place for merchants dealing in goods, bills of exchange and shipping, and helped make Hamburg a leading centre of northern European trade.

hamburg-america-line.s: The Hamburg America Line (HAPAG) was a shipping company founded in Hamburg in 1847 to carry passengers and mail across the Atlantic. Under Albert Ballin it became the largest shipping company in the world by 1914, carrying millions of emigrants to the Americas.

harburg-wilhelmsburg.s: Harburg-Wilhelmsburg was a Prussian city on the south bank of the Elbe, formed in 1927 by merging the industrial towns of Harburg and Wilhelmsburg. A centre of rubber, oil and port industries, it was incorporated into Hamburg by the Greater Hamburg Act of 1937, and its two…

helmut-schmidt.s: Helmut Schmidt (1918–2015) was a German Social Democratic politician who was chancellor of West Germany from 1974 to 1982. As Hamburg's senator for the interior he won national fame for directing rescue work during the North Sea flood of 1962.

heinrich-von-zutphen.s: Heinrich von Zütphen (1488–1524) was a Dutch Augustinian friar and follower of Martin Luther. Having escaped imprisonment in the Netherlands, he began preaching in Bremen in 1522 and won the city for the Reformation.

hassi-messaoud.s: Hassi Messaoud is a town in the north-eastern Algerian Sahara that grew around one of Africa's largest oil fields, discovered in 1956 as French Algeria entered its final crisis. The Sahara's oil and gas made control of the desert a major issue in the independence negotiations,…

hussein-dey.s: Hussein Dey (c. 1765–1838) was the last dey of the Regency of Algiers, ruling from 1818 to 1830. In 1827, during a dispute over debts owed by France for grain, he struck the French consul Pierre Deval with a fly-whisk, giving France a pretext for a naval blockade.

hoang-hoa-tham.s: Hoàng Hoa Thám, known as De Tham, was a Vietnamese resistance leader who held out against the French for almost three decades in the hills of Yên Thế in northern Vietnam. After intermittent fighting and truces with the colonial authorities, he was killed in 1913, and his long…

halfaya.s: Halfaya, or Halfayat al-Muluk, is a town on the east bank of the Nile north of the confluence of the Blue and White Niles, now part of Khartoum North in Sudan. In the later Funj period it became the seat of the Abdallab shaykhs, the chief vassals of Sennar, who had earlier…

hambach-festival.s: The Hambach Festival was a mass demonstration held from 27 to 30 May 1832 at Hambach Castle near Neustadt in the Bavarian Palatinate, where some 20,000 to 30,000 people called for German national unity, freedom of the press and popular sovereignty. The black, red and gold flag…

hadiqat-al-haqiqa.s: The Hadiqat al-Haqiqa, or Walled Garden of Truth, is a long didactic poem by the Persian poet Sana'i of Ghazni, completed around 1131 and dedicated to the Ghaznavid sultan Bahram Shah. Combining ethics, theology and mystical teaching with anecdotes, it was the first great Sufi…

hasanak.s: Hasanak was the vizier of the Ghaznavid sultan Mahmud of Ghazni from about 1024 and a supporter of Mahmud's son Muhammad in the succession dispute of 1030. After Mas'ud I took the throne, Hasanak was accused of heresy for having received a robe from the Fatimid caliph and was…

huanren.s: Huanren is a county in Liaoning province in north-eastern China, on the Hun River near the border with North Korea. Korean tradition places Jolbon, the first capital of Goguryeo, in this area, and the nearby Wunü Mountain fortress is usually identified with it.

hwando.s: Hwando was a mountain fortress capital of the Korean kingdom of Goguryeo, near modern Ji'an in Jilin province, China, paired with the walled city of Gungnae in the plain below. It was sacked in 244 by the Cao Wei general Guanqiu Jian and in 342 by the Former Yan.

hyeja.s: Hyeja was a Buddhist monk from the Korean kingdom of Goguryeo who came to Japan in 595. According to the Nihon shoki he became the teacher of Prince Shotoku, the regent of Empress Suiko, and helped to establish Buddhism at the Yamato court.

haeju-choe-clan.s: The Haeju Choe clan is a Korean lineage that rose to prominence in the Goryeo period through the scholar and chief minister Choe Chung. It was one of the great capital-based aristocratic families that intermarried with the royal house and held high office in the eleventh and…

haeinsa.s: Haeinsa is a major Buddhist temple on Mount Gaya in South Gyeongsang province, South Korea, founded in 802. Since 1398 it has kept the Tripitaka Koreana, more than 81,000 woodblocks of the Buddhist canon carved in the thirteenth century.

heungdeoksa.s: Heungdeoksa was a Buddhist temple in Cheongju, Korea, where in 1377 the Jikji, the oldest surviving book printed with movable metal type, was produced. The temple disappeared, and its site was identified only by excavations in the 1980s.

hyeonjong-of-goryeo.s: Hyeonjong of Goryeo was king of Goryeo from 1009 to 1031. Brought to the throne after a coup, he faced the Khitan invasion of 1010, which burned Kaegyong and forced him to flee south to Naju.

heinrich-von-gagern.s: Heinrich von Gagern was a German liberal politician from the Grand Duchy of Hesse. In March 1848 he became the grand duchy's chief minister, and in May he was elected president of the Frankfurt National Assembly, the first freely elected parliament for all Germany.

hessian-ludwig-railway.s: The Hessian Ludwig Railway was a private railway company of the Grand Duchy of Hesse, named after Grand Duke Louis III. Founded in 1845 and based in Mainz, it built lines linking Mainz with Worms, Darmstadt, Frankfurt and the Rhineland.

house-of-nassau.s: The House of Nassau is a German noble dynasty named after Nassau Castle on the Lahn, which split in 1255 into a Walramian and an Ottonian line. The Ottonian branch produced the princes of Orange-Nassau, stadtholders and later kings of the Netherlands, while the Walramian…

harishena.s: Harishena was a court poet and minister of the Gupta emperor Samudragupta in the fourth century CE. He composed the Prayaga prashasti, the Sanskrit eulogy inscribed on the Allahabad Pillar, which lists Samudragupta's conquests of kings in northern and southern India and the…

henry-kamen.s: Henry Kamen is a British historian of Spain, born in Burma in 1936. His books, including The Spanish Inquisition, Spain's Road to Empire and biographies of Philip II and Philip V, challenged traditional views of Spanish decline and of the Inquisition.

helsingborg.s: Helsingborg is a port city in Scania, southern Sweden, on the narrowest point of the Øresund opposite Helsingør in Denmark. Danish for most of the Middle Ages, its castle guarded the Sound, and in 1362 Valdemar IV defeated a Hanseatic fleet off the town.

hildebrand-veckinchusen.s: Hildebrand Veckinchusen was a Hanseatic merchant based mainly in Bruges, who with his brother Sivert traded furs, cloth, salt and spices between Flanders, Livonia, Lübeck and, briefly, Venice. Several hundred letters and account books of the family survive in the archives of…

hispania-citerior.s: Hispania Citerior, "Nearer Spain", was the Roman province created in 197 BCE from Rome's conquests along the Mediterranean coast of eastern Iberia after the Second Punic War. Its governors extended Roman rule inland through the Celtiberian and Lusitanian wars.

hoysaleswara-temple.s: The Hoysaleswara Temple at Halebidu, the former Hoysala capital Dwarasamudra in Karnataka, is a twin-shrined temple to Shiva begun around 1121 during the reign of Vishnuvardhana. Built of soapstone on a star-shaped platform, it is covered with friezes and thousands of carved…

himayat-sagar.s: Himayat Sagar is a reservoir on the Esi river near Hyderabad, completed in 1927 under the Nizam Osman Ali Khan and named after his son Azam Jah, Himayat Ali Khan. With the Osman Sagar, it was built after the disastrous Musi flood of 1908 to protect the city from floods and…

hyderabad-contingent.s: The Hyderabad Contingent was a military force paid for by the Nizam of Hyderabad but commanded by British officers, raised in the early 19th century to support the British subsidiary force in the Deccan. Its cost led the Nizam to assign the revenues of Berar to the British in…

hyderabad-state-congress.s: The Hyderabad State Congress was a political party founded in 1938 to campaign for responsible government in Hyderabad State. Banned by the Nizam's government, it led satyagraha campaigns, and under Swami Ramananda Tirtha it pressed in 1947–1948 for accession to India.

haldimand-proclamation.s: The Haldimand Proclamation was a decree issued on 25 October 1784 by Frederick Haldimand, governor of the Province of Quebec, granting the Six Nations of the Iroquois a tract of land six miles deep on each side of the Grand River in present-day Ontario. It rewarded those who…

hiawatha-belt.s: The Hiawatha Belt is a wampum belt of purple and white shell beads that records the founding of the Haudenosaunee (Iroquois) Confederacy. Its four squares and central tree stand for the five original nations, linked by a line, with the Onondaga, keepers of the central council…

hudson-river.s: The Hudson River flows about 500 kilometres south from the Adirondack Mountains of New York to the Atlantic at New York City. Named after Henry Hudson, who sailed up it for the Dutch in 1609, its valley was the core of New Netherland and the route between New York and Albany.

han-shizhong.s: Han Shizhong was a general of the Song dynasty and one of the leading commanders who defended the Southern Song against the Jurchen Jin. In 1130 his fleet blockaded a Jin army returning north at Huangtiandang on the Yangtze for over forty days.

han-tuozhou.s: Han Tuozhou was a chief minister of the Southern Song dynasty, related by marriage to the imperial family, who dominated the court from the 1190s. He banned the teachings of Zhu Xi as 'false learning' and in 1206 launched a war to recover northern China from the Jin.

hall-of-worthies.s: The Hall of Worthies (Jiphyeonjeon) was a royal research institute of Joseon, enlarged by King Sejong in 1420 as a centre of scholarship. Its young scholars studied Chinese institutions and classics, advised the king and compiled works on history, agriculture, medicine and…

heungseon-daewongun.s: Heungseon Daewongun, Yi Ha-eung, was the father of King Gojong and regent of Joseon from 1864 to 1873. He strengthened the throne by curbing the in-law clans, closing most private Confucian academies and rebuilding Gyeongbokgung.

hong-gyeong-naes-rebellion.s: Hong Gyeong-nae's Rebellion was an uprising in Pyeongan province in north-western Korea from December 1811 to the spring of 1812. Led by Hong Gyeong-nae, an educated man barred from office, it drew on resentment of the region's exclusion from government posts, on merchants and…

hunminjeongeum.s: The Hunminjeongeum ('Correct Sounds for the Instruction of the People') is the document by which King Sejong of Joseon promulgated the Korean alphabet, now called Hangul, in 1446. The alphabet of 28 letters, created in 1443, was designed so that ordinary people could write…

hwaseong-fortress.s: Hwaseong Fortress is a walled fortress surrounding the centre of Suwon in South Korea, built from 1794 to 1796 by King Jeongjo near the relocated tomb of his father, Crown Prince Sado. Its walls run for about 5.7 kilometres with gates, bastions and towers, and its builders…

hummay.s: Hummay was a king of Kanem near Lake Chad in the late eleventh century and the founder of the Sayfawa dynasty, which ruled Kanem and later Bornu until the nineteenth century. Kanem tradition, including a charter of privileges known as his mahram, holds that he adopted Islam,…

haqnazar-khan.s: Haqnazar Khan was khan of the Kazakhs from 1538 to 1580 and a son of Qasim Khan. Coming to power after a period of defeats and internal strife, he restored Kazakh power over the steppe, fought the Moghuls and Oirats in the east and pushed west into former Nogai pastures as the…

hilarion-of-kiev.s: Hilarion was the first metropolitan of Kiev of native Rus' origin, appointed by Yaroslav the Wise in 1051 without waiting for the patriarch of Constantinople. Before that he was a priest at the prince's church at Berestovo near Kiev.

hisham-i-of-cordoba.s: Hisham I was the second Umayyad emir of Córdoba, ruling from 788 to 796, son of Abd al-Rahman I. A pious ruler who favoured the Maliki school of law, he sent annual summer campaigns against the Christian north, sacking Oviedo in 794 and 795, and raided Septimania in 793.

herrenchiemsee.s: Herrenchiemsee is a palace on the island of Herreninsel in the Chiemsee, Bavaria's largest lake, built for Ludwig II from 1878 as a tribute to Louis XIV and modelled on Versailles. Its hall of mirrors is longer than the original.

historical-commission-bavarian-academy.n: Historical Commission at the Bavarian Academy of Sciences
historical-commission-bavarian-academy.s: The Historical Commission at the Bavarian Academy of Sciences was founded in Munich in 1858 by Maximilian II of Bavaria, with the historian Leopold von Ranke as its first chairman. It became one of the leading institutions of German historical scholarship, publishing editions…

henri-alexis-brialmont.s: Henri Alexis Brialmont was a Belgian military engineer and general, the leading fortress designer of his age. He planned the fortifications of Antwerp as the national redoubt and, in the 1880s, the rings of concrete forts around Liège and Namur.

herge.s: Hergé was the pen name of Georges Remi, a Belgian cartoonist best known for "The Adventures of Tintin", which began in 1929. His clear-line drawing style shaped the Franco-Belgian comics tradition, and the series was translated into dozens of languages.

henry-colvile.s: Henry Colvile was a British army officer who served as acting commissioner of the Uganda Protectorate from 1893 to 1895. At the end of 1893 he led British-officered troops and a large Ganda army into Bunyoro against Omukama Kabalega, occupying much of the kingdom and building…

hans-christian-andersen.s: Hans Christian Andersen was a Danish writer, born in Odense, best known for his fairy tales, among them "The Little Mermaid", "The Ugly Duckling", "The Emperor's New Clothes" and "The Snow Queen". He also wrote novels, plays, poems and travel books.

helsingor.s: Helsingør is a town in north-eastern Zealand, Denmark, at the narrowest point of the Øresund, opposite Helsingborg in Sweden. From around 1429 until 1857 Danish kings levied the Sound Toll there on ships passing between the North Sea and the Baltic.

henry-i-count-of-schwerin.s: Henry I, called the Black, was Count of Schwerin in northern Germany. In May 1223 he seized King Valdemar II of Denmark and his eldest son on the island of Lyø and held them prisoner, releasing them only in 1225 for a large ransom and the surrender of most German conquests.

house-of-commons-of-england.s: The House of Commons of England was the lower house of the Parliament of England, made up of knights of the shire and burgesses elected from the towns. It began to sit apart from the Lords in the fourteenth century, and its consent became necessary for taxation.

house-of-hanover.s: The House of Hanover was a German princely dynasty, electors and later kings of Hanover, that ruled Great Britain and Ireland from 1714 to 1901. The English Act of Settlement of 1701 fixed the succession on Sophia of Hanover, a Protestant granddaughter of James I, and her son…

henry-dundas.s: Henry Dundas, later 1st Viscount Melville, was a Scottish lawyer and politician who dominated the management of Scottish politics for about three decades in the late eighteenth century. A close ally of William Pitt the Younger, he presided over the Board of Control for India…

henry-fielding.s: Henry Fielding was an English novelist, playwright and magistrate. His satirical plays helped provoke the Licensing Act of 1737, after which he turned to the novel, writing Joseph Andrews and The History of Tom Jones, a Foundling (1749), comic works that helped shape the…

hawarden-castle.s: Hawarden Castle is a ruined medieval castle in Flintshire, north-east Wales, near the English border. A stone castle was built there in the thirteenth century on an earlier Norman site.

hexham.s: Hexham is a market town in Northumberland, England, on the River Tyne. Around 674 Wilfrid founded a monastery there whose church, built with stone from Roman sites, was among the finest in Anglo-Saxon England; its crypt survives under the present Hexham Abbey.

holyhead.s: Holyhead, in Welsh Caergybi, is a port town on Holy Island off the west coast of Anglesey in north Wales. It grew around a small Roman fort and a church founded by Saint Cybi in the sixth century, which became an important clas church of medieval Gwynedd.

hugh-of-montgomery-2nd-earl-of-shrewsbur.n: Hugh of Montgomery, 2nd Earl of Shrewsbury
hugh-of-montgomery-2nd-earl-of-shrewsbur.s: Hugh of Montgomery was a Norman nobleman, son of Roger of Montgomery, who became Earl of Shrewsbury in 1094. With Hugh, Earl of Chester, he campaigned in north Wales against Gruffudd ap Cynan.

holy-crown-of-hungary.s: The Holy Crown of Hungary is the coronation crown of the Hungarian kings, traditionally linked with Stephen I, though its surviving form combines Byzantine enamel work of the later eleventh century with a Latin upper part. From the later Middle Ages it embodied the kingdom…

hormizd-iv.s: Hormizd IV was king of the Sasanian Empire from 579 to 590. Son of Khosrow I, he waged wars against Byzantium and the Turks, and around 580 he abolished the monarchy of Iberia, governing it through a Persian official.

henry-grattan.s: Henry Grattan was an Irish politician and orator who led the Patriot opposition in the Irish Parliament. Backed by the Volunteers, he won the repeal of the Declaratory Act and the amendment of Poynings' Law in 1782, giving the Irish Parliament legislative independence, a…

holon.s: Holon is a city on the central coastal plain of Israel, immediately south of Tel Aviv, founded in the 1930s. Besides its industry and residential districts, it is one of the two centres of the Samaritan community, alongside Mount Gerizim near Nablus; Samaritans settled there…

hoshea.s: Hoshea was the last king of Israel, reigning from about 732 to 722 BCE. He came to power by killing Pekah and submitted to Tiglath-pileser III as an Assyrian vassal, but later withheld tribute and sought help from Egypt.

hild-of-whitby.s: Hild of Whitby (c. 614–680) was a Northumbrian princess and abbess, baptised with her great-uncle King Edwin in 627. In 657 she founded the double monastery of Whitby, which she ruled until her death and which trained several bishops.

haakon-the-good.s: Haakon the Good (c. 920–961) was king of Norway from about 934, the youngest son of Harald Fairhair. Raised as a Christian at the court of Æthelstan of England, he returned to displace his half-brother Eric Bloodaxe.

henrik-ibsen.s: Henrik Ibsen (1828–1906) was a Norwegian playwright, often called the father of modern drama. After early verse dramas such as Brand and Peer Gynt, written in Italian exile, he turned to realistic prose plays that examined the morals of middle-class society, among them A…

hirlas-owain.s: Hirlas Owain ('Owain's Drinking Horn') is a Welsh poem of the late twelfth century attributed to Owain Cyfeiliog, prince of southern Powys. Set at a feast after a raid, it has the prince call on his cupbearer to fill the long blue horn for each of his warriors in turn,…

humboldt-university-of-berlin.s: The Humboldt University of Berlin was founded in 1810 as the University of Berlin on the plans of Wilhelm von Humboldt, as part of the Prussian reforms after the defeat by Napoleon. It joined teaching with free research, a model copied by universities in Germany, the United…

hutu-manifesto.s: The Hutu Manifesto was a document written in March 1957 by nine Hutu intellectuals, among them Grégoire Kayibanda, and addressed to the Belgian colonial authorities in Rwanda. It denounced the Tutsi monopoly of political, economic and educational power and demanded advancement…

house-of-savoy.s: The House of Savoy is a dynasty founded in the early eleventh century by Humbert I, Count of Savoy, in the western Alps. It became dukes of Savoy in 1416, ruled Piedmont from Turin, took the royal title of Sicily in 1713 and exchanged it for Sardinia in 1720.

holyrood-abbey.s: Holyrood Abbey is a ruined abbey of Augustinian canons in Edinburgh, founded by David I in 1128. Kings often stayed in its guesthouse, which developed into the Palace of Holyroodhouse, the royal residence that still stands beside the ruins.

hats-party.s: The Hats were one of the two political parties of Sweden's Age of Liberty, dominated by the nobility and officers and in power from 1738 to 1765. They favoured mercantilist economic policies and an alliance with France aimed at reversing Swedish losses to Russia, which led to…

house-of-sverker.s: The House of Sverker was a royal dynasty of medieval Sweden, founded by Sverker the Elder, who became king around 1130. For about a century its kings alternated on the throne with the rival House of Eric, and several of them died violently in the struggles between the two…

house-of-representatives-netherlands.s: The House of Representatives, or Second Chamber (Tweede Kamer), is the lower and more powerful house of the States General of the Netherlands, created when the parliament became bicameral in 1815. Directly elected since the constitution of 1848, it has had 150 members chosen…

hilton-of-cadboll-stone.s: The Hilton of Cadboll Stone is a Pictish cross-slab of about 800 from Easter Ross in northern Scotland. Its surviving face shows a hunting scene with a woman riding side-saddle, trumpeters and animals, framed by vine-scroll and Pictish symbols; the cross on the other side was…

hermann-hesse.s: Hermann Hesse was a German-born Swiss novelist and poet, born at Calw in Württemberg. His novels, including Siddhartha (1922), Steppenwolf (1927) and The Glass Bead Game (1943), explore spiritual search and individual identity.

hermann-von-mittnacht.s: Hermann von Mittnacht was a Württemberg statesman who dominated the kingdom's government after German unification, serving as minister of justice from 1867 and as head of the ministry from 1876 to 1900. A moderate conservative, he worked closely with Bismarck while defending…

hmannan-yazawin.s: The Hmannan Yazawin, or Glass Palace Chronicle, is the official chronicle of the Burmese monarchy, compiled by a committee of scholars appointed by King Bagyidaw in 1829 and completed in 1832. Drawing on earlier chronicles and inscriptions, it narrates the history of the…

hsinbyumashin.s: Hsinbyumashin was a Burmese queen, one of the senior queens of King Mindon, who dominated the court at the end of his reign. With her daughter Supayalat and allied ministers she secured the succession of Thibaw in 1878, and the massacre of royal princes and princesses that…

henrique-of-kongo.s: Henrique was a son of King Afonso I of Kongo, educated in Portugal, who in 1518 was made a bishop with the approval of Pope Leo X, the first bishop from sub-Saharan Africa. He returned to Kongo in 1521 as titular bishop of Utica and auxiliary bishop for the kingdom, but ill…

helios.s: Helios is the god of the sun in Greek religion, pictured driving a chariot across the sky. He was the patron god of Rhodes, where the Colossus of Rhodes represented him and annual priests of Helios gave their names to the year.

hermaeus.s: Hermaeus was one of the last Indo-Greek kings, ruling in the Paropamisadae around the Kabul valley in the early 1st century BCE. His silver and bronze coins, showing the king and the enthroned Zeus, were imitated for decades after his death by Indo-Scythian and Yuezhi rulers.

huvishka.s: Huvishka was a Kushan emperor who succeeded Kanishka and reigned for about three decades in the middle of the 2nd century CE, when the empire stretched from the Amu Darya to the middle Ganges. His abundant gold coinage shows the widest range of gods of any Kushan ruler, and…

haw-phra-kaew.s: Haw Phra Kaew is a temple in Vientiane, Laos, built by King Setthathirath around 1565 to house the Emerald Buddha, which he had brought from Lan Na. The Siamese took the image to Thailand in 1779, and the temple was destroyed in the sack of Vientiane in 1828.

hoang-ngu-phuc.s: Hoàng Ngũ Phúc was a general of the Trịnh lords who ruled northern Vietnam. Taking advantage of the Tây Sơn rebellion against the Nguyễn lords, he led a Trịnh army south and captured the Nguyễn capital Phú Xuân in 1775, briefly extending Trịnh rule over the centre of the…

harbel.s: Harbel is a town in Margibi County, Liberia, the headquarters of the Firestone rubber plantation established in 1926, one of the largest in the world. It was named after Harvey and Idabelle Firestone.

hermigar.s: Hermigar was a king of the Suebi in Hispania in the early 5th century. In 429, as the Vandals under Gaiseric prepared to cross to Africa, his Suebi were plundering Lusitania; the Vandals defeated him near Emerita Augusta (Mérida), and he drowned in the Guadiana while fleeing.

history-of-the-patriarchs-of-alexandria.n: History of the Patriarchs of Alexandria
history-of-the-patriarchs-of-alexandria.s: The History of the Patriarchs of Alexandria is a collection of biographies of the Coptic patriarchs of Alexandria, compiled in Arabic in Egypt from the 11th century and traditionally attributed to Severus ibn al-Muqaffa. Drawing on earlier Coptic sources and extended by later…

house-of-ascania.s: The House of Ascania is a German princely dynasty named after Aschersleben in Saxony-Anhalt. Albert the Bear founded the Margraviate of Brandenburg in 1157, and his descendants ruled it until the line died out in 1320, extending German settlement east of the Elbe.

havelland.s: The Havelland is a region of Brandenburg, Germany, west of Berlin, enclosed by the loops of the Havel river. Home of the Slavic Hevelli, whose stronghold was Brandenburg an der Havel, it passed to Albert the Bear in 1150 and became a core territory of the Margraviate of…

hutterites.s: The Hutterites are an Anabaptist Christian community that holds property in common, named after Jakob Hutter, a leader burned for heresy at Innsbruck in 1536. Fleeing persecution in Tyrol, they built communal settlements on noble estates in Moravia in the 16th century, but…

hodonin.s: Hodonín is a town in South Moravia, Czech Republic, on the Morava river at the border with Slovakia. It was the birthplace in 1850 of Tomáš Garrigue Masaryk, the first president of Czechoslovakia.

hamengkubuwono-i.s: Hamengkubuwana I, earlier Prince Mangkubumi, was the founder and first sultan of Yogyakarta. A son of Amangkurat IV, he rebelled against his brother Pakubuwana II and the Dutch East India Company in 1746, and the Treaty of Giyanti of 1755 divided Mataram between him and…

heliopolis-ancient-egypt.s: Heliopolis, Egyptian Iunu and biblical On, was one of the oldest cities of ancient Egypt, now within north-eastern Cairo, and the chief cult centre of the sun god Ra and of Atum. Its priesthood developed an influential creation theology.

henenu.s: Henenu was an Egyptian official, chief steward under the Eleventh Dynasty kings Mentuhotep II and Mentuhotep III. An inscription in the Wadi Hammamat records that in Mentuhotep III's eighth year he led an expedition of some 3,000 men across the Eastern Desert to the Red Sea,…

heqanakht.s: Heqanakht was an Egyptian landowner and funerary priest of the early Middle Kingdom, known from a group of letters and accounts found in a tomb near Deir el-Bahari at Thebes. Written while he was away from home, the Heqanakht Papyri give detailed instructions on fields, rents,…

hecatomnid-dynasty.s: The Hecatomnid dynasty ruled Caria in south-west Asia Minor as satraps of the Persian Empire in the 4th century BCE. Founded by Hecatomnus of Mylasa, it reached its height under his son Mausolus, who moved the capital to Halicarnassus and extended Carian power over Rhodes and…

humayuns-tomb.s: Humayun's Tomb in Delhi is the mausoleum of the Mughal emperor Humayun, commissioned by his widow Bega Begum and completed around 1572. Designed by the Persian architect Mirak Mirza Ghiyas, it was the first great garden tomb of the Indian subcontinent, set in a walled…

heinrich-himmler.s: Heinrich Himmler was Reichsführer of the SS from 1929 and from 1936 chief of all German police, including the Gestapo. He built the SS into a state within the state that ran the concentration camps, and he was the principal organiser of the Holocaust and of the murder of…

hitler-youth.s: The Hitler Youth was the youth organisation of the Nazi Party, founded in 1926. After 1933 rival youth groups were banned, and from 1939 membership was compulsory for boys aged 10 to 18, while girls joined its branch, the League of German Girls.

hjalmar-schacht.s: Hjalmar Schacht was a German banker who as currency commissioner helped end the hyperinflation of 1923 and was president of the Reichsbank in 1923–1930 and 1933–1939. As Hitler's economics minister from 1934 to 1937 he financed rearmament with the secret Mefo bills, but he…

hochelaga.s: Hochelaga was a fortified St Lawrence Iroquoian village on the island of Montreal, visited by Jacques Cartier in October 1535. Cartier described a palisaded town of about fifty longhouses surrounded by cornfields and named the nearby hill Mount Royal.

helen-clark.s: Helen Clark is a New Zealand politician who was Prime Minister from 1999 to 2008, leading the Fifth Labour Government through three terms. She was the first woman elected Prime Minister at a general election.

henri-riviere.s: Henri Rivière was a French naval officer and writer. Sent to Tonkin in 1882, he seized the Hanoi citadel in April of that year, provoking a crisis with the Vietnamese court and China.

hiarbas.s: Hiarbas was a king of Numidia in the early first century BCE, installed after the expulsion of Hiempsal II with the backing of the Marian faction in Rome's civil war. When Sulla's lieutenant Pompey invaded Africa in 81 BCE, he defeated the Marian commander Gnaeus Domitius…

hiempsal-ii.s: Hiempsal II was king of Numidia from about 88 BCE until around 60 BCE, a son of King Gauda and the father of Juba I. Driven out by the Marian faction during Rome's civil wars, he was restored by Pompey in 81 BCE and ruled thereafter as a loyal Roman client.

hippo-regius.s: Hippo Regius was an ancient city on the coast of present-day Algeria, on the site of modern Annaba. A Phoenician foundation, it became one of the royal residences of the Numidian kings and then a major Roman port and city.

hans-holbein-the-younger.s: Hans Holbein the Younger was a German-born painter and printmaker who worked in Basel and England and is regarded as one of the greatest portraitists of the sixteenth century. In Basel he painted Erasmus and designed woodcuts, including The Dance of Death.

helvetic-republic.s: The Helvetic Republic was a unitary state established in Switzerland after the French invasion of 1798 and proclaimed at Aarau on 12 April 1798. It abolished the sovereignty of the cantons and the subject territories and introduced equality before the law, but it remained…

htilominlo.s: Htilominlo, also called Nadaungmya, was king of Pagan from 1211 to 1235, chosen by his father Narapatisithu from among several sons. He completed the Gawdawpalin Temple and built the Htilominlo Temple, among the last of the great temples of Pagan.

hecatompylos.s: Hecatompylos, Greek for 'hundred gates', was an ancient city in north-eastern Iran, identified with the ruins of Shahr-e Qumis near Damghan. It lay on the main road from Media to Central Asia, was taken by Alexander the Great in 330 BCE, and served as an early capital and…

house-of-suren.s: The House of Suren was one of the great noble families of Parthian and Sasanian Iran, with its estates in Sakastan, the present-day Sistan. Under the Arsacids its head held the hereditary right to crown the king, and its most famous member, the general Surena, destroyed the…

hainan.s: Hainan is a large tropical island in the South China Sea, off the southern coast of Guangdong, and the southernmost province of the People's Republic of China. Long a remote place of exile under the imperial dynasties, it was taken from the Nationalists by the People's…

hanyu-pinyin.s: Hanyu Pinyin is the official system for writing Standard Mandarin Chinese in the Latin alphabet, adopted by the People's Republic of China in 1958 and developed by a committee that included the linguist Zhou Youguang. It is used to teach pronunciation and to type Chinese…

hu-jintao.s: Hu Jintao is a Chinese politician who was general secretary of the Chinese Communist Party from 2002 to 2012 and president of the People's Republic of China from 2003 to 2013. Trained as a hydraulic engineer, he rose through the party in western provinces.

huaihai-campaign.s: The Huaihai campaign was one of the three decisive campaigns of the Chinese Civil War, fought from November 1948 to January 1949 in the region around Xuzhou between the Huai River and the Longhai railway. Communist armies under Liu Bocheng, Chen Yi and Deng Xiaoping destroyed…

herstal.s: Herstal is a town on the Meuse just north of Liège, Belgium. In the early Middle Ages it was a residence of the Carolingian family, the home of Pepin of Herstal, and from the early modern period it was a centre of arms manufacture, home since 1889 of the Fabrique Nationale (FN…

henry-iv-of-castile.s: Henry IV was king of Castile from 1454 to 1474. His reign was marked by noble rebellion and disputes over the legitimacy of his daughter Joanna, and he was briefly offered the crown of Catalonia in 1462.

humor-monastery.s: Humor Monastery is an Orthodox monastery in Suceava County, Romania. Its church was built in 1530 by the chancellor Teodor Bubuiog with the support of Prince Petru Rareș, and its outer frescoes of 1535 make it one of the painted churches of northern Moldavia on the UNESCO…

hadim-suleiman-pasha.s: Hadım Suleiman Pasha was an Ottoman commander and governor of Rumelia under Mehmed II. In January 1475 he led a large Ottoman army into Moldavia and was decisively defeated by Stephen the Great at the Battle of Vaslui.

house-of-movila.s: The House of Movilă was a Moldavian boyar family that gave the principality several princes around 1600, notably Ieremia Movilă (1595–1606) and Simion Movilă, who ruled with Polish backing in rivalry with Michael the Brave and Ottoman candidates. The family built Sucevița…

herophilus.s: Herophilus of Chalcedon was a Greek physician who worked in Alexandria under the early Ptolemies and is often called the father of anatomy. He was among the first to perform systematic dissections of human bodies, distinguished nerves from tendons, described the brain, the eye…

hong-kong-island.s: Hong Kong Island is an island on the south side of Victoria Harbour, at the mouth of the Pearl River in southern China. Occupied by Britain in 1841 during the First Opium War and ceded by the Treaty of Nanjing in 1842, it became the core of the colony of Hong Kong, with its…

hasan-agha.s: Hasan Agha was a Sardinian-born convert and eunuch who rose in the service of Hayreddin Barbarossa and governed Algiers as his deputy from 1533. In October 1541 he led the defence of the city against the great expedition of Charles V, whose fleet was wrecked by a storm and…

hasan-pasha-son-of-hayreddin.s: Hasan Pasha was a son of Hayreddin Barbarossa who served three terms as Ottoman beylerbey of Algiers between 1544 and 1567. He extended Algerian control westwards against the Saadians of Morocco and the Spanish, but failed to take the Spanish strongholds of Oran and Mers…

hernan-siles-zuazo.s: Hernán Siles Zuazo was a Bolivian politician, a founder of the Revolutionary Nationalist Movement (MNR) and a leader of the revolution of 1952. He was president from 1956 to 1960, when he imposed a stabilisation plan, and again from 1982 to 1985, when he restored democracy…

hugo-banzer.s: Hugo Banzer was a Bolivian general who ruled as dictator from 1971, when he seized power in a coup, until 1978. His regime, backed by business and the United States, banned parties and unions and persecuted opponents, while the economy grew on loans and commodity exports.

hu-shi.s: Hu Shi was a Chinese philosopher, essayist and diplomat, a student of John Dewey and a leader of the New Culture Movement. His essays of 1917 called for literature written in the vernacular rather than classical Chinese, a change that transformed Chinese writing.

hms-beagle.s: HMS Beagle was a Royal Navy brig-sloop launched in 1820 and converted for survey work. On her second voyage, from 1831 to 1836 under Captain Robert FitzRoy, she surveyed the coasts of South America and sailed round the world, carrying the young naturalist Charles Darwin, whose…

helsinki-final-act.s: The Helsinki Final Act was signed on 1 August 1975 in Helsinki by 35 states, including the United States, Canada, the Soviet Union and almost all European countries, at the end of the Conference on Security and Co-operation in Europe. It recognised the inviolability of…

house-of-visconti.s: The House of Visconti was the noble family that ruled Milan from the late thirteenth century until 1447, first as lords and from 1395 as dukes. Under Gian Galeazzo Visconti they built a state covering much of northern Italy and threatened Florence, and they also held Genoa at…

haitian-creole.s: Haitian Creole is a French-based creole language spoken by almost the whole population of Haiti. It developed in the colony of Saint-Domingue from the eighteenth century among enslaved Africans of many languages, combining mostly French vocabulary with grammatical influences…

hurricane-fifi.s: Hurricane Fifi was a tropical cyclone that skirted the north coast of Honduras in September 1974, bringing torrential rain that caused catastrophic flooding and landslides. It killed an estimated 3,000 to 10,000 people, most of them in Honduras, and destroyed much of the…

hurricane-iota.s: Hurricane Iota was a Category 4 Atlantic hurricane that struck the Caribbean coast of Nicaragua on 16 November 2020, less than two weeks after Hurricane Eta had hit the same area. Moving across Nicaragua and Honduras, it caused severe flooding and landslides that, together…

hull-alfaro-treaty.s: The Hull–Alfaro Treaty was signed in 1936 by US Secretary of State Cordell Hull and the Panamanian envoy Ricardo J. Alfaro, and ratified by the United States in 1939. It revised the Hay–Bunau-Varilla Treaty by ending the American guarantee of Panama's independence and the…

hay-bunau-varilla-treaty.s: The Hay–Bunau-Varilla Treaty was signed on 18 November 1903 by US Secretary of State John Hay and Philippe Bunau-Varilla, acting for the newly independent Panama. It granted the United States in perpetuity a zone ten miles wide across the isthmus to build and run a canal, in…

hay-herran-treaty.s: The Hay–Herrán Treaty was signed in January 1903 by US Secretary of State John Hay and the Colombian chargé d'affaires Tomás Herrán. It would have allowed the United States to build a canal across Panama, then part of Colombia, in a zone leased for 100 years.

hugo-spadafora.s: Hugo Spadafora was a Panamanian physician and guerrilla fighter who served in the government of Omar Torrijos and fought in Nicaragua, first with the Sandinistas and later against them. A vocal critic of Manuel Noriega, whom he accused of drug trafficking, he was seized and…

henry-meiggs.s: Henry Meiggs was an American railway builder who, after fleeing debts in San Francisco in 1854, built railways in Chile and then Peru. From 1870 he undertook Peru's great railway programme, including the Central Railway from Callao and Lima across the Andes, one of the highest…

holy-league-1571.s: The Holy League of 1571 was an alliance against the Ottoman Empire formed by Pope Pius V with Spain, the Republic of Venice, Genoa, Savoy, the Knights of Malta and other Italian states. Its fleet, commanded by Don John of Austria, destroyed the Ottoman navy at the Battle of…

holy-league-1684.s: The Holy League of 1684 was an alliance against the Ottoman Empire formed after the relief of Vienna by Pope Innocent XI with the Holy Roman Emperor Leopold I, the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth and Venice; Russia joined in 1686. In the Great Turkish War its armies recovered…

holy-league-1511.s: The Holy League of 1511 was an alliance formed by Pope Julius II with Venice, Spain and later England, the Swiss and the Holy Roman Emperor, to drive the French out of Italy during the War of the League of Cambrai. Despite a French victory at Ravenna in 1512, Swiss and allied…

hanish-islands.s: The Hanish Islands are a group of volcanic islands in the southern Red Sea between Yemen and Eritrea. Eritrea seized the largest, Greater Hanish, in December 1995, and the dispute was taken to international arbitration.

hussein-badreddin-al-houthi.s: Hussein Badreddin al-Houthi was a Zaydi religious leader and former member of the Yemeni parliament who founded the movement that bears his family's name. From the Saada region he preached against Western and Saudi influence and the government of Ali Abdullah Saleh.

houthi-movement.s: The Houthi movement, officially Ansar Allah, is a Zaydi Shia political and armed movement from the Saada region of northern Yemen, named after its founder Hussein Badreddin al-Houthi. After six wars with the government from 2004 to 2010, it seized Sanaa in September 2014 with…

hluttaw.s: The Hluttaw was the royal council of chief ministers in pre-colonial Burma, which handled administration, justice and royal decrees under the Toungoo and Konbaung dynasties. Its ministers, the wungyi, met in a hall within the palace and could act on the king's behalf.

hermen-rode.s: Hermen Rode was a painter based in Lübeck, one of the leading artists of the Hanseatic world in the late 15th century. His surviving works include the high altar of St Nicholas' Church in Tallinn (Reval), completed in 1481, and the St Luke altarpiece in Lübeck, showing the…

hinton-st-mary-mosaic.s: The Hinton St Mary Mosaic is a fourth-century Roman floor mosaic found in 1963 at Hinton St Mary in Dorset, England. Its central roundel shows the head of a man in front of the chi-rho monogram, widely thought to be one of the earliest known images of Christ.

hero-of-alexandria.s: Hero of Alexandria was a Greek mathematician and engineer who worked in Alexandria in the first century CE. His surviving works describe machines driven by air, water and steam, among them the aeolipile, a simple steam turbine, as well as automata, surveying instruments and a…

hypatia.s: Hypatia was a Neoplatonist philosopher, mathematician and astronomer in Alexandria, the daughter of the mathematician Theon. She taught philosophy to pagan and Christian pupils and advised the city's leaders.

heliand.s: The Heliand is an Old Saxon epic poem of about 6,000 lines, written around 830, that retells the life of Christ from the Gospels in Germanic alliterative verse. It presents Christ as a lord and his disciples as loyal retainers, adapting the story to the values of the recently…

hesychasm.s: Hesychasm is a tradition of contemplative prayer in Eastern Orthodox monasticism that seeks inner stillness (hesychia) and the vision of divine light through constant repetition of the Jesus Prayer. Defended by Gregory Palamas and upheld by Byzantine church councils in the…

hanukkah.s: Hanukkah is an eight-day Jewish festival beginning on 25 Kislev, usually in December. It commemorates the rededication of the Temple in Jerusalem in 164 BCE by Judas Maccabeus and his followers, after the Seleucid king Antiochus IV Epiphanes had desecrated it.

houmuwu-ding.s: The Houmuwu ding is a rectangular bronze cauldron of the late Shang dynasty, found at Anyang in Henan in 1939. Weighing about 830 kilograms, it is the heaviest bronze vessel known from ancient China.

huan-river.s: The Huan River is a river in northern Henan, China, that flows east through the city of Anyang. The late Shang capital at Yinxu lay on its banks, with the palace and temple area on the south side and the royal cemetery at Xibeigang to the north, and the earlier walled city of…

huanbei-shang-city.s: Huanbei Shang City is the site of a large walled city of the middle Shang period on the north bank of the Huan River near Anyang, Henan. Discovered in 1999, its square enclosure, about two kilometres on each side, contains large palace foundations.

humaid-bin-abdullah-al-qasimi.s: Humaid bin Abdullah Al Qasimi was ruler of Ras al-Khaimah from 1869 to 1900. A member of the Qasimi family, he made Ras al-Khaimah independent of Sharjah, and it was treated as a separate sheikhdom under British protection during his reign.

hari-singh-nalwa.s: Hari Singh Nalwa was a commander of the Sikh Empire under Maharaja Ranjit Singh. He took part in the conquests of Kasur, Multan, Kashmir and Peshawar, and served as governor of Kashmir and later of the Peshawar frontier, where he built forts against Afghan attacks.

hwangnam-daechong.s: Hwangnam Daechong is the largest Silla tomb at Gyeongju, South Korea, a double burial mound of the fifth century about 120 metres long, probably of a king and his queen. Excavated in 1973–1975, it contained tens of thousands of objects, among them a gold crown, glassware from…

hyecho.s: Hyecho was a Buddhist monk from Silla who studied in Tang China and in the 720s travelled to India, visiting the holy places of Buddhism and returning through Central Asia. His account, Memoir of a Pilgrimage to the Five Kingdoms of India, was lost until a fragment was found…

hyegong-of-silla.s: Hyegong was king of Silla from 765 to 780, coming to the throne as a child. His reign saw repeated revolts by noble factions, and he was killed in a rebellion in 780.

hwaeom.s: Hwaeom is the Korean branch of the Huayan school of Buddhism, based on the Avatamsaka Sutra and its teaching of the interdependence of all things. It was founded by the monk Uisang, who studied in Tang China and returned to Silla around 670, and Buseoksa was among its main…

ha-giang-province.s: Ha Giang was a mountainous province in the far north of Vietnam, bordering China, with a population largely of ethnic minorities such as the Hmong and Tày. Its Vi Xuyen district saw heavy border fighting with China between 1984 and 1989.

haidar-abu-bakr-al-attas.s: Haidar Abu Bakr al-Attas is a Yemeni engineer and politician who became head of state of South Yemen after the civil war of January 1986, serving until the unification of 1990. He was then the first prime minister of the unified Republic of Yemen, and in the civil war of 1994…

heracleidae.s: The Heracleidae were, in Greek myth, the descendants of the hero Heracles. Their legendary return to the Peloponnese, led by Temenus, Cresphontes and Aristodemus, was used by the Greeks to explain the arrival of the Dorians, who took Argos, Messenia and Laconia.

henryk-sienkiewicz.s: Henryk Sienkiewicz was a Polish novelist and winner of the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1905. He is best known for Quo Vadis and for his historical novels, among them the Trilogy set in seventeenth-century Poland and The Teutonic Knights (Krzyżacy, 1900), which culminates in…

hermann-von-salza.s: Hermann von Salza was Grand Master of the Teutonic Order from 1210 to 1239. A trusted adviser of Emperor Frederick II who also mediated between the emperor and the papacy, he obtained the Golden Bull of Rimini and papal grants that founded the Order's state in Prussia.

house-of-wonders.s: The House of Wonders, Beit al-Ajaib, is a ceremonial palace in Stone Town, Zanzibar, built for Sultan Barghash bin Said and completed in 1883. It was the first building in East Africa to have electricity and a lift, and was damaged in the British bombardment of 1896.

hamad-bin-thuwaini.s: Hamad bin Thuwaini was Sultan of Zanzibar from 1893 to 1896, ruling under the British protectorate. A grandson of Said bin Sultan through Thuwaini, ruler of Muscat, he was chosen with British approval.

heligoland-zanzibar-treaty.s: The Heligoland–Zanzibar Treaty was signed on 1 July 1890 between Britain and Germany. Germany recognised a British protectorate over Zanzibar and Pemba and British interests in East Africa and gave up claims in Witu, while Britain ceded the North Sea island of Heligoland to…

henck-arron.s: Henck Arron was a Surinamese politician and leader of the National Party of Suriname who served as prime minister from 1973 to 1980. He led the country to independence from the Netherlands on 25 November 1975 and negotiated a large Dutch aid settlement.

havelock-mine.s: The Havelock mine was an asbestos mine at Bulembu in north-western Eswatini, worked from 1939 to 2001. For decades it was one of the largest asbestos mines in the world and a major source of Swaziland's export earnings, linked to Barberton in South Africa by a long aerial…

hilda-kuper.s: Hilda Kuper was a social anthropologist born in Southern Rhodesia who spent much of her career studying the Swazi. Her books, including An African Aristocracy (1947), on rank and ritual in the kingdom, and a biography of Sobhuza II, remain the classic accounts of Swazi…

henry-dunant.s: Henry Dunant was a Swiss businessman and humanitarian from Geneva. Shocked by the suffering of wounded soldiers after the Battle of Solferino in 1859, he wrote A Memory of Solferino, which called for neutral relief societies and an international agreement to protect the wounded.

hoffmann-la-roche.s: Hoffmann-La Roche, usually known as Roche, is a Swiss pharmaceutical and diagnostics company founded in Basel in 1896 by Fritz Hoffmann-La Roche. It grew out of the Basel chemical tradition into one of the largest pharmaceutical firms in the world, known for products such as…

hayashi-razan.s: Hayashi Razan was a Japanese Neo-Confucian scholar who served the first four Tokugawa shoguns as adviser and drafter of documents. A follower of the teachings of Zhu Xi, he promoted a philosophy of hierarchical social order and loyalty that suited the new regime.

house-of-romanov.s: The House of Romanov was the dynasty that ruled Russia from the election of Michael Romanov as tsar in 1613 until the abdication of Nicholas II in 1917. Descended from a Muscovite boyar family related to Ivan IV through his first wife Anastasia, it produced Peter the Great,…

hammir-singh.s: Hammir Singh was a ruler of Mewar who recovered Chittor from the governors of the Delhi Sultanate around 1326 and founded the Sisodia branch of the Guhila dynasty, taking the title of rana. Head of the Sisodia family, a cadet line named after the village of Sisoda, he rebuilt…

hill-forts-of-rajasthan.s: The Hill Forts of Rajasthan are a group of six forts inscribed together as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2013: Chittorgarh, Kumbhalgarh, Ranthambore, Gagron, Amber and Jaisalmer. Built and enlarged by Rajput states between the eighth and eighteenth centuries, they use hills,…

holy-spirit-movement.s: The Holy Spirit Movement was a rebel movement in northern Uganda led by Alice Auma, known as Alice Lakwena, an Acholi spirit medium who claimed guidance from a spirit called Lakwena. Recruiting mainly Acholi soldiers of the defeated former army, it fought Yoweri Museveni's…

harold-wilson.s: Harold Wilson was a British Labour politician who served as prime minister from 1964 to 1970 and from 1974 to 1976. His governments faced repeated economic crises, devalued the pound in 1967 and announced in January 1968 the withdrawal of British forces from east of Suez,…

hmt-empire-windrush.s: HMT Empire Windrush was a passenger ship, built in Germany in 1930 as the Monte Rosa, that brought more than a thousand passengers, most of them from the Caribbean, to Tilbury in June 1948. Its arrival became a symbol of post-war Commonwealth migration to Britain, and the…

human-rights-act-1998.s: The Human Rights Act 1998 is a law of the United Kingdom that incorporated the rights of the European Convention on Human Rights into domestic law. In force from October 2000, it allows people to bring rights cases in British courts and requires public bodies to respect…

hms-dreadnought-1906.s: HMS Dreadnought was a Royal Navy battleship launched in 1906 whose design, with a uniform main armament of ten 12-inch guns and steam-turbine propulsion, made all earlier battleships obsolete. Her name became the term for a new class of capital ship, and her launch intensified…
